speechtext: wish to direct a question to the Minister of Justice. Can he inform the house whether he will take steps to stop any death sentences being carried out until such time as parliament gives consideration to the findings of the special joint committee on capital punishment?

speakeroldname: Hon. Stuart S. Garson (Minister of Justice):
speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: REQUEST FOR SUSPENSION UNTIL CONSIDERED BY PARLIAMENT
speechtext: I wish to thank my hon. friend for giving me notice of his question. The governor general in council, in his present consideration of the question of commutation of sentences of death, carries out the laws of Canada in their present form. Until parliament amends the present law with regard to capital punishment the governor in council should not, in my view, by executive action, attempt to bring about in effect a change in the law, which only parliament can lawfully make.

subtopic: REQUEST FOR SUSPENSION UNTIL CONSIDERED BY PARLIAMENT
speechtext: May I ask a supplementary question of the Minister of Justice. Is the minister aware that in Great Britain the operation of the statute was suspended while capital punishment was under consideration in the House of Lords?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: REQUEST FOR SUSPENSION UNTIL CONSIDERED BY PARLIAMENT
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, my understanding of what happened in the United Kingdom is that for a short period in the year 1948 death sentences were commuted to life imprisonment. The sole reason that was given for the decision to recommend those commutations was the position resulting from the vote in the House of Commons on the clause in the criminal justice bill suspending capital punishment for five years. This was not because a royal commission or a joint committee of parliament was investigating the matter. The royal commission in England which reported on capital punishment was in fact appointed in 1949 and reported in 1953. During this period there was no suspension of capital punishment, nor were there any commutations granted for other than the usual reasons under the royal prerogative of mercy.

speakeroldname: Hon. Douglas Abbolt (Minisler of Finance) moved
speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: PROVISION FOR DECENNIAL REVISION, EXTENSION OF CHARTERS, ETC.
speechtext:
that the house go into committee to consider the following resolution:
That it is expedient to introduce a measure to provide for the decennial revision of the Bank Act and the extension of the charters of the existing chartered banks till July 1, 1964, and to provide further for certain changes in connection with the administration of the act.
Motion agreed to and the house went into committee, Mr. Robinson (Simcoe East) in the chair.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: PROVISION FOR DECENNIAL REVISION, EXTENSION OF CHARTERS, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, the bill to be based upon this resolution provides for the decennial revision of the Bank Act. It extends the charters of the eleven chartered banks for a ten-year period from July 1 of this year. In accordance with the practice

The Bank Act
on similar occasions in the past, I am recommending a new act and the repeal oi the one now in force.
At this time I wish to draw to the attention of hon. members the proposals contained in this bill for some of the more important changes in the present legislation. These are:
A provision that if parliament is not sitting during the 30 days preceding July 1, 1964, the charters will be extended until 60 days after the commencement of the next session.
A provision to increase the amount of capital which a newly-incorporated bank must have before it commences business. The present requirements were enacted in 1890 and are considered inadequate under present-day conditions.
A change relating to the issue by a bank of additional capital stock, which is intended to remove some of the obstacles which now exist.
A change regarding investments eligible for the pension fund of a bank.
A provision permitting each bank to determine the method by which ownership in shares of its capital stock may be transferred. At present this can only be done by registration on the books of the bank.
A change in the method of computing cash reserves of a bank and in the minimum ratio of cash reserves to deposit liabilities. This provision is complementary to the amendment proposed to the Bank of Canada Act which I explained at some length on second reading of that bill. Together, they are intended to give the Bank of Canada a better control of the reserves of chartered banks.
A provision which prohibits the issue of notes intended for circulation outside of Canada and terminates all note-issuing rights of the banks.
A provision complementing the amendment to the National Housing Act and permitting a bank to make loans on the security of insured mortgages.
A provision to clarify the lending powers of a bank on the security of oil in the ground and in transit. The banks have taken a very active part in the development of the oil and related industries in Canada and have been instrumental in providing them with substantial financing from time to time. The proposed revisions specify the type of loans which may be made to assist this comparatively new but very important part of our economy and the security which may be taken.
Changes in the provisions regarding amalgamations, to conform with current legislation and business practice.
Provision for payment from the consolidated revenue fund to the Bank of Canada of all unclaimed deposits of defunct banks, thereby placing with the bank all deposits of this kind.
There will be many consequential changes arising from those I have mentioned and others of less importance. I shall deal with these in greater detail, of course, on second reading and, when that stage is concluded, will move that the bill be referred to the standing committee on banking and commerce.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR DECENNIAL REVISION, EXTENSION OF CHARTERS, ETC.

However, I can tell him that the principal changes, the changes which involve any departure from previous policy, are those which I have indicated in the brief statement I have just given.

Mr. Chairman, it is not our intention to say anything at this stage of the resolution. More will be heard from us later. I should like to ask the minister if he is in position to put on Hansard a statement similar to that
[Mr. Abbott.)

which was put on Hansard by the Right Hon. Mr. Ilsley, as appears at page 2550 of the 1944 debates of the House of Commons. That was headed "statement of current operating earnings and expenses and other information for the ten chartered banks."

subtopic: PROVISION FOR DECENNIAL REVISION, EXTENSION OF CHARTERS, ETC.
speechtext: Of course that information could be made available. My recollection is that the 1944 revision of the act was not preceded by a resolution-why, I do not know. Perhaps it is because of the inclusion in the Bank Act of some provisions which were formerly in the Bank of Canada Act, but it was decided by the law officers of the crown that this bill should be preceded by a resolution. I shall give consideration to my hon. friend's question and see whether I can cover that in my second reading speech or whether it might be more appropriately made available in the banking and commerce committee. The information he has asked for can be made available and will be made available if desired.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR DECENNIAL REVISION, EXTENSION OF CHARTERS, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I am going to
be just a little different from the representatives of the other two parties. I do not intend to speak at any length, but I use as justification for taking a few minutes of the time of the committee a rather important point which is involved. I hope what I shall have to say may perhaps induce the minister when he is making his statement on the motion for second reading to get to grips with the one important point I shall raise, and by that method we can perhaps deal with the question at issue and do something about it.
I was interested to learn of the scope of the changes which are proposed in the new act, and I was glad to see that something is to be done to enable chartered banks to take certain securities and make provision for financing oil development. That is an important thing in our province. It will be of importance, I believe, in several of the other western provinces also, and it seems to me necessary to make it possible for the chartered banks to assist in that development. I was also interested in some of the other things the minister said, but I shall confine myself more to the question of the change in the minimum cash reserves, as related to the change in the Bank of Canada Act.
I do not believe, Mr. Chairman, that a more important bill ever comes before parliament than the measure providing for the decennial revision of the Bank Act and the extension of the bank charters. This act, coupled with the Bank of Canada Act, lays down fundamental financial policy for Canada, and every 83276-169J
The Bank Act
aspect of that policy has a profound effect upon the lives, liberties and fortunes of every man, woman and child in the country.
For that reason the greatest care should be exercised in dealing with this measure which the minister proposes introducing today. It should be subjected to the minutest scrutiny and to most careful consideration by members of parliament both here and in the banking and commerce committee to which I understand it will be sent.
Our view in regard to all this banking legislation was very well expressed by the hon. member for Acadia when he spoke in the debate on the second reading of the Bank of Canada Act on February 25. He said in effect, though these are not his exact words, that we do not want the amendments dealing with the cash reserves of the chartered banks to be too restricted in degree to permit the government to institute what we consider to be a sound financial policy, that will encourage the optimum development of our resources and permit the equitable distribution of the goods and services resulting from that development. Most hon. members will agree, I believe he said, that during any long period of peace that has not been the case. Consequently, there is real need and room for considerable improvement.
At this point, Mr. Chairman, I hasten to say that we-I do not like to interrupt the conversations which are taking place between hon. members, Mr. Chairman, as I like to allow them their peace, but I do believe it is in the interests of all hon. members that we have some order.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR DECENNIAL REVISION, EXTENSION OF CHARTERS, ETC.
speechtext:
I hasten to say at this point, Mr. Chairman, that we believe our Canadian branch banking system is one of the best banking systems in the world. We believe the Canadian chartered banks have done a very fine job of financing production, which is of course the major responsibility imposed upon them by their charters. We believe they have managed their affairs quite admirably and have maintained a standard of safety and liquidity which is very high by comparison with any other system in the world.
We are just as anxious as anyone else to see that our chartered banks maintain their enviable position in these and other respects which could be mentioned. We would like to see them privately-owned and we hope they will never become government-owned institutions. We do not take too seriously

The Bank Act
the declarations we sometimes hear that they will be nationalized under other administrations.
Governments of the past in Canada have given the chartered banks a virtual monopoly of money creation and issue. This monopoly of the chartered banks can and does exercise a tremendous power of control over every phase of private and national business. The manner in which they exercise that control determines to a very large degree whether our country enjoys prosperity or suffers adversity.
Authorities list about nine major factors affecting the economy which determine whether we have boom and depression or steady prosperity. I would like to name these nine factors, because I believe they must enter into any consideration we might give the Bank Act. They are these: debts, currency volume, price level, net worth, profit, production, psychology, currency turnover, which some people call rate of flow of currency, and rate of interest.
Of late years many outstanding authorities have come to believe that eight of these factors can be influenced by regulating the volume of deposit money in this country. The chartered banks are almost if not completely in control of deposit money. It is within their sole discretion to grant or refuse loans, which is the means, of course, by which deposit money is brought into existence.
It is true that the cash reserves against which loans are made are created and issued by the Bank of Canada. By varying the volume of this cash reserve the Bank of Canada can limit the volume of deposit money, but it can only use influence in the matter of increasing the volume of deposits. I stress that important point.
Deposit money becomes effective demand when it is immediately available to buy goods and services. By varying the volume of deposits, therefore, the chartered banks may create or diminish effective demand, sometimes with good and sometimes with drastic results. I would like to quote a short example of what can happen in this respect. This quotation is contained in a remarkable booklet by De Vee Lee, entitled, "Twentieth Century Economic System." Perhaps some hon. members have already seen this little booklet. This is the quotation:
When the effective demand for goods is increased so suddenly and largely that current production cannot be speeded up fast enough to keep up with it, stocks begin to diminish and prices to rise. The first impetus upwards may be given by a relatively small increase in demand from the ultimate consumer, or it may be due to psychological causes. The upward movement, when once started, is, however, carried forward by the urgent and largely increased demands of the holder of stocks, whether

manufacturer, wholesale dealer or retail trader. His action is based on fear and greed: the fear that if he does not buy now, prices will go still higher, and the hope that if he does buy now, prices will go still higher and he will reap the benefits. The result of his action is, in fact, to drive prices higher. When prices are falling, he holds off the market in the fear that if he buys now, his competitor will later buy at lower prices, and the hope that if he does hold off, prices will go lower. The effect of his holding off is to drive prices lower. This psychological factor could, it is submitted, be reversed and made to work in favour of stability.
When such uneconomic price fluctuations are set in motion, Mr. Chairman, the chartered banks, advised and assisted, of course, by the Bank of Canada, set about devising remedial action. What do they do under present circumstances? Again I would like to quote the author of "Twentieth Century Economic System" to illustrate what they do. The author states:
The technique under which the Bank of England-
And I understand the technique and procedure of the central bank of Canada is approximately the same.
-contracted the cash base of the joint stock banks, so compelling them-if they were to maintain their ratio of cash to deposits-to reduce their deposit by calling in loans, was always effective in stopping the boom and forcing down prices. The trouble arose when the prices reached the point of equilibrium and then passed it and the major slump supervened. Existing technique was incapable of stopping the fall in prices at the point of equilibrium. It was for this reason that the monetary authorities hesitated to check an upward rise in prices at its inception. They might so easily convert an incipient boom into an uncontrollable major slump.
There is the big problem under the system and policy as they now exist in Canada, how to stop a contraction of the volume of deposit money at the point of equilibrium and prevent the economy from going into a real depression. As I say, that is the real weakness of the present policy and mechanism.
I should like to take a brief look at what would happen in Canada when, after some reluctance-and I say that advisedly because I believe the Bank of Canada would approach this matter with considerable reluctance-the Bank of Canada would set about counteracting an inflationary danger by contracting the cash reserves of the chartered banks. They have that authority now under the amendment to the Bank of Canada Act. It is possible for them to contract from 12 per cent to 8 per cent or to increase from 8 per cent to 12 per cent. We do not believe that is quite enough, but at any rate for the time being it is a step in the right direction. When cash reserves are reduced by the Bank of Canada, the banks have to call in loans to enable them to meet their obligations. Producers, distributors and traders might therefore be forced to throw their stocks and their

goods onto an unwilling market in order to get the money to repay the loans. Soon a surplus of unsaleable goods might be overhanging the whole market, and very likely would be. What was a drama in the upsurge of a boom becomes a tragedy.
If effective demand could now be increased to absorb the surplus goods, of course everything would be well. But this the banks could not do under present policy. They can only increase purchasing power by making loans to producers or distributors; but the deflationary policy will already have rendered many former customers uncreditworthy. Those who are still creditworthy would not want to borrow or produce more when they could not sell what they had already produced.
That is the stalemate. What we need in our policy is a mechanism for stopping the downward movement brought on by a contraction of the cash reserves, stopping it at the point of equilibrium, in order to prevent depression. The only mechanism that can do that, as far as I can see, is one by which new purchasing power can be put directly into the hands of ultimate consumers so they can immediately make it effective demand and halt the downward trend.
I am hoping that such a mechanism will be provided in the bill which the minister brings in. He did not say anything about it today. Of course I did not expect him to go into detail at this stage, and I shall be quite content to wait until I have a chance to examine the bill. I mention this matter now in order to get the minister thinking about the thing that is in my mind and, I believe, in the minds of those whom I represent. The trouble now is that, to save their own skins in a deflationary movement ordered by the Bank of Canada, the chartered banks feel that they have to take away, as one man put it, the parasol just when it starts to rain, and the rest of us get soaked.
I shall not speak longer at this stage. We shall have more to say on second reading of the bill when we know more about what is in it. I shall close by simply stating that inasmuch as the chartered banks enjoy a monopoly of money issue, it is only reasonable to expect that when the national interest requires an increase in money supply to meet the distributive need and to keep economic activity and employment at a high level, the banks will make that money available at a reasonable rate of interest. I think that would not be expecting too much in the light of the substantial profits shown by the banks over the years.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, some years ago I brought to the attention of my hon. colleagues the fact that in order to understand our banking system one should look at the Canada Gazette and the annual reports of the banks. They are sent upon request, but I wonder how many members of parliament have asked for them. They are extremely interesting, and they represent the practical side of banking.
There are many theories about banking, debt and credit. Everyone will realize that credit is just debt. However, there are debts that are an asset from the other point of view. Assets and liabilities are convertible. What I mean by that is that when there is an asset somewhere, there is a liability on the other side. But what interests me particularly is a tabulation that was published under date of January 26, 1954, in the Canada Gazette and which appeared in the issue of February 6. It shows the liabilities of the eleven chartered banks in Canada. I have not the report of the Mercantile Bank of Canada, which is a new one, but I have the reports of the other ten chartered banks.
The total liabilities of the banks is $10,715,915,936. On the other hand, these are the liquid assets of the Canadian people. They represent deposits by and balances due to the dominion government; deposits by and balances due to provincial governments; advances from the Bank of Canada, secured; deposits by the public, payable on demand, in Canada, in Canadian currency; deposits by the public, payable after notice or on a fixed day, in Canada, in Canadian currency; deposits in Canada, in currencies other than Canadian; deposits elsewhere than in Canada; deposits by and balances due to other chartered banks in Canada; deposits by and balances due to banks and banking correspondents in the United Kingdom; deposits by and balances due to banks and banking correspondents elsewhere than in Canada and the United Kingdom; acceptances and letters of credit outstanding; liabilities to the public not included under the foregoing heads; dividends declared and unpaid; rest or reserve fund; capital paid up; and finally, total of foregoing liabilities.
This tabulation seems to be arid, but it is extremely interesting. In order to discuss the banking business sensibly we must get down to brass tacks and consider those official returns and available information about banking in general. With regard to theories of banking, I have my personal views which I shall have another opportunity to expound. But what strikes me is that our banks compare favourably with the banks of any other

The Bank Act
country. The dean of Canadian banks, the Bank of Montreal, was founded in the early 1800's. It has made its 136th annual report, which means that the bank has carried on business for 136 years. Very few United States institutions could compare with it. There was a time when the banks of our powerful and very rich neighbour were falling down and our banks were standing up and rendering great service to the public. Let me mention the opinion of Mr. Gordon R. Ball, president of the Bank of Montreal, about the revision of the bank charters. He said:
I earnestly hope that two basic considerations will be kept clearly in mind. One is that a competitive banking system, operating with the minimum of formal restrictions, has been amply shown by experience to be best suited to the needs of the Canadian community. The other is that both competition and flexibility can be most effective when they proceed from a position of strength. It would be doing an ill favour to the Canadian public unnecessarily to fetter the banks in the performance of their functions. And it would be no less dangerous, in pursuit of any doctrinaire notions, to push the banks into a position in which they were expected to assume risks, wholly inconsistent with their duty as guardians of other people's money, which they must be prepared at all times to pay.
This statement deserves serious consideration. Those who have read the report have found very appropriate remarks about "constructive banking", "a flexible monetary policy", "an opportunity to be seized", "the role of the United States", "Canada's responsibilities", and so on. The president of the Bank of Montreal suggests prudent optimism with regard to the future. I also commend to the attention of my hon. colleagues the remarks made by the general manager of the Bank of Montreal.
If we take the second oldest bank, the Bank of Nova Scotia, it has made its I22iiu annual report, which means that the bank has carried on operations for 122 years. This is also a very fine record, and I hope that hon. members who received the report of that bank have read it. The title of the address delivered by Mr. H. L. Enman, president of the bank, is "Canadian Development is Unequalled in Free World". This is remarkable. Think of it, sir. The president of an institution like the Bank of Nova Scotia told the shareholders of the bank at the annual meeting that Canadian development is unequalled in the free world. This is a matter for thought. He also made remarks under the headings "Canada has come a long way since before the war", "High investment and consumer buying main features of 1953", and so on.
I am not going to read all he said about the outlook because all my colleagues are familiar with what has been said, but I draw their attention to another part of the address

in which he dealt with the underlying growth of the Canadian economy. Mr. C. Sydney Frost, general manager of the Bank of Nova Scotia, delivered an address entitled "Production Growth Big Factor in Increased Bank Lending". This means that loans by the banks have been made wisely. Very often when someone goes to his bank manager to ask for a loan he is told that the matter will be referred to the head office. Naturally the banks must be cautious. They must show the prudent optimism or optimistic prudence referred to by one of these bankers. These men are human. They started at the bottom of the ladder. My hon. friends know very well that it is the practice of bank presidents to employ their sons in the banks as messengers in the first place and then in better positions, in order that they may be familiar with the whole banking structure. They meet other young men, become friends with them, and they learn their profession. They know their business, and that is the reason our banks have survived for so long.
I have referred to the two oldest banks. If we take the reports of all the other banks we will see that we have every reason to be proud of our banking system. I know that sometimes I have made requests to the banks that have been refused. They have to make such decisions, but that is no reason not to declare to the Canadian people that they must have entire confidence in our banking system inasmuch as our bankers have a free hand. For a time the Bank of Canada rendered very bad service to the lumbering industry when they cut their credit short, resulting in reduced operations. One of the reasons we have to amend the Unemployment Insurance Act is so that those engaged in forestry operations may have something to live on during the winter because those carrying on lumbering operations cannot get credit at their own banks on account of the instructions that were given by the Bank of Canada.
I have great respect for those gentlemen who consider that banking is a position of trust and confidence. They act in a very democratic fashion. They have annual meetings at which they meet their shareholders who are all invited to attend, and they give them any information asked for about the management at large of the banks. I could mention all the other banks. I have their reports here. I must not read long extracts, but I shall summarize the reports of the eleven chartered banks by saying that these men who are the pillars of finance in this country have confidence in the future of Canada and they are ready to help all

those who come with serious representations to get credit in order to promote their own businesses.
But, here again, it is impossible for the banks to accede to all requests and grant all that is asked for. It cannot be done. On the other hand, however, management of the banks in Canada has been wise; and the proof of this is that the banks have survived the years of depression and other difficulties. Now they are prosperous, and everybody knows it.
The report of the Canadian Bank of Commerce is very encouraging. Then if we look at the report of the Royal Bank of Canada we find something of particular interest in the address of the president, Mr. James Muir, and also the address of Mr. Atkinson, general manager of the bank. They have published separately reviews of conditions in Canada and in other countries. If our trade is progressing by leaps and bounds it is due, in the first place, to the initiative of the Minister of Trade and Commerce, who has done so much to help our fellow citizens who are engaged in business, and due also to the facilities and opportunities offered by the banks.
I could mention also many other banks, including the Bank of Toronto, the Canadian Bank of Commerce, and the Royal Bank. We find, too, a very interesting report from the Dominion Bank which makes reference to business conditions, mortgage lending and matters of that kind. These are things that should be looked into. Some banks publish in their annual reports lists of their branches throughout the country-and not only that, but in other countries as well. This is interesting, because they have afforded a number of facilities to Canadian exporters and importers.
The president of the Imperial Bank of Canada has said that the real output has expanded. He, too, has a message of cheer, as have also the two French-Canadian banks, namely La Banque Provinciale du Canada and Banque Canadienne Nationale.
I was also keenly interested in the report of Barclays Bank. My idea of banking is that the money deposited in banks in Canada should serve the Canadian people, and should not be sent outside. The danger with Barclays Bank is that it is a subsidiary of Barclays Bank, Limited, of London, and it is impossible to know what amount of Canadian money has been sent from Canada to the United Kingdom through that bank.
The Bank Act
I had a question on the order paper, which was passed as an order for return, in which I asked for information about the assets of the fire insurance companies. These are powerful companies; some of them are American, some English and some Canadian. I would like to know if the assets of these fire insurance companies, made up of money from the Canadian people, are serving Canadian business. Information on this point is of more importance than a discussion of any theory, because so long as the money coming from the pockets of the Canadian people is in the hands of the banks, it should be used to promote Canadian business. I shall have more to say about that in the debate on second reading.
If Canadian business is prosperous now it is due to several factors. It is due to the initiative of the Minister of Finance as well as that of the Minister of Trade and Commerce and other members of the government, including the Prime Minister, together with the initiative of those who are in the banks. And when I refer to the banks I do not refer only to those who work in bank offices. I refer to all those Canadian businessmen who have offices from one coast to the other, as far out as Newfoundland, men who are public spirited, who try to do the best they can with their own businesses and who, at the same time, are ready to help all Canadians with initiative who wish to make a success of any enterprise in which they are engaged.
I must add that bank customers are also an asset. The Canadian people should be very happy to have a banking system like ours, where there are no bank failures, and where the banks are good servants of the people.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: PROVISION FOR DECENNIAL REVISION, EXTENSION OF CHARTERS, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, my colleague the hon. member for Winnipeg North indicated when he spoke some few minutes ago that we were prepared to have the debate on this legislation, so far as policy is concerned, take place on second reading of the bill. From what I have said I do not want it to be understood that we offer any criticism of the last two speakers for taking advantage of the opportunity to speak now. However, in view of the more extended remarks that have now been made, it seems to me that perhaps a further brief statement might be made upon our behalf.
So far as these various stages of debate are concerned, no one can lay down a hard and fast rule as to whether debate should take place at the resolution or at the bill

The Bank Act
stage. As a matter of fact the practice varies from one piece of legislation to another. This legislation is somewhat complicated, and we shall certainly have much more to say when the bill is before us and the debate on second reading takes place.
However, since a few statements that might be regarded as of a policy nature are being made, I think it should be made clear that it is our view, as was expressed on February 25 by my leader when the bill amending the Bank of Canada Act was before us, that public ownership and control of the commercial banks is necessary if we are going to have complete control by the people over fiscal and monetary policies. We recognize and contend that those who control fiscal and monetary policies exercise tremendous control over the lives of our people. We are glad that some steps in the right direction have been taken. I refer to the fact that we have a central bank, and I refer also to such controls as we have over the chartered banks through the medium of the Bank Act.
We feel, however, that more social controls than we have yet achieved are necessary, and that eventually at any rate this calls for public ownership of the commercial banks. We feel, too, that it calls for social or public control of the flow of investment.
As I have already indicated, we are prepared to have the major debate on the matter when we reach second reading stage, when we shall develop our position more fully. I did feel that, in view of the somewhat extended remarks that were made by the last two speakers, we should not let this stage go by without it being made very clear that our position is still the one we have taken in the past, namely public ownership, as my leader pointed out in the debate last week on the bill amending the Bank of Canada Act.

speechtext:
I was quite interested in the remarks made by the hon. member for Temis-couata. I gathered from his remarks that he was referring to the insurance companies and banks. He tried to imply that money received by insurance companies should be all kept in this country. I am sure he is not aware of the fact that before a foreign insurance company can start doing business in this country they must deposit with the federal government a substantial sum of money, sufficient in the minds of the government and others who have had years of experience to protect the policyholders.
Foreign companies, and particularly the British companies of which he spoke, have been established here for years and have spent millions of dollars in this country. Only

recently a company took out a charter in Canada. The money of that company came from Switzerland. They purchased a large office building on St. James street in Montreal for something like $1 million. That company has already purchased bonds and securities in this country to the extent of millions of dollars. That same company has purchased the Buffalo Insurance Company of Buffalo, New York, for approximately $6 million. The Canadian company with head office in Canada is reaping the benefit of operating in the United States, and is bringing thousands and thousands of dollars back to this country.
I believe that if we tried to put the clamps on foreign insurance companies and others that are interested in investing in Canada, it would be a great mistake. They are entitled to earn a return on the money they have invested in the development of Canada. I do not think it behooves us to criticize foreign companies that choose to come here and make a start and endeavour to ultimately become something worth while and participate in the wealth of this country, if they help in the building up of the country.
Nobody can deny that the original companies, particularly the British companies, were instrumental in the building up of Canada's vast financial and other resources. They have contributed in a large way to the development of Canada. Barclays Bank was mentioned. I am sure that before Barclays Bank were permitted to operate in this country they were carefully scrutinized by the federal government. They are building up their position, and anybody who deposits money in that bank does so with his eyes open. They are not a small institution, and if they decide to take any money which may be deposited with them and invest it in some other part of the world, I am sure the stockholders and depositors will be satisfied with the returns they may receive either as depositors or stockholders.
I do not think foreign financial institutions should be criticized unless we have something positive to go on, unless we have some reason for saying that they are detrimental to the Dominion of Canada, that we do not want them here and that we want to enact laws which are going to try to make them invest in Canada every cent received.
It would be utterly impossible to cover the insurance requirements of Canada with Canadian insurance companies. We must have foreign insurance companies. Approximately $28 million a year in reinsurance money is taken by Lloyd's on insurance risks in Canada. Therefore we want to make sure those people who are taking the initial risk in investing in our financial institutions such as insurance companies and banks are protected. It would

be a mistake to try to force them to invest all their money in Canada. They have invested in Canada for hundreds of years, and Canada has reaped the benefit.

speechtext:
I think the hon. member for Peace River made a very important point in his comment. That was that there is no assurance that when the nation is facing the possibility of a recession the chartered banks will do that which is in the interest of the nation at that time, namely make the borrowing of money easier. As a matter of fact the banks usually do the very opposite thing to that which is in the interest of the nation. When we are in a period of inflation it is usually quite easy for the citizens of the nation to obtain loans from the chartered banks in very large quantities.
The hon. member for Peace River came down, as I expected he would, on the side opposed to public ownership; but he did point out to the chartered banks now privately owned that if they were to fulfil their obligations to the nation they would need to exercise sound lending policies, particularly when the nation was facing a recession.

speechtext:
The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre restated the position of the C.C.F. movement, namely that the chartered banks of this nation should be publicly owned and controlled. If that were done there is no question in my mind but that the right kind of lending policies would be undertaken by the chartered banks, so that an impending recession and depression could be averted.
I do not expect-no one in this house does -this government to adopt a policy of public ownership of the banking system of this nation. I do, however, believe the Minister of Finance is anxious that the chartered banks, whenever the country is facing the possibility of a recession, should adopt those policies that will help avert a recession. I believe the Minister of Finance would like to see the chartered banks of Canada undertake a policy of making loans whenever prices are falling and the nation seems to be headed for a depression.
Perhaps there is another means by which such a laudable objective might be achieved. I am thinking of the vast and valuable credit movement that has grown up from one end of Canada to the other, particularly in recent years. With the adoption in this house last year of a measure to provide for a central credit union for the deposit of funds on hand in individual credit unions, I believe the credit union movement is year by year becoming more financially sound. I am hoping
The Bank Act
that the minister and the government, along with the credit union movement of this country, will work out some arrangement whereby the credit unions in Canada can obtain some of the rights and prerogatives now enjoyed by the chartered banks in Canada.
I know as a primary producer that even though under our present banking legislation in Canada the chartered banks are given absolute guarantees against losses on such things as farm improvement loans, nevertheless in a good many instances the chartered banks do not lend the money to producers who really need such funds, and the reason is well known. Unless a primary producer, the same as any other potential customer of the bank, can prove to the satisfaction of the bank manager that he is in a very sound financial position, the chances are that he will go away without the loan. The credit union movement, without any guarantee from the federal government, has lent money to tens of thousands of Canadian citizens who were unable to get money from the chartered banks of Canada even though that money from the chartered banks would be lent on iron-clad guarantees against loss by the federal government.
Even though the credit unions have undertaken what would be normally high-risk loans, nevertheless in my opinion they are in very sound financial condition. I think co-operative ownership is one of the best possible types of ownership. I should like to see closer co-operation between the government and the credit union movement so that step by step our credit unions may be given the same rights and guarantees that are now provided for the chartered banks. If that is done I am sure that the credit unions would then be prepared to lend money in such a way as to assist the government in a fiscal policy aimed at avoiding a depression.
I have far greater faith in credit unions and the ability of people who operate credit unions to lend money wisely at a smaller loss than I have even in our well-established chartered banks. I think that by bringing the credit unions into the same category as our chartered banks and giving them the same rights the government not only would be supporting the co-operative movement, a most valuable movement, but would have one additional and powerful means of avoiding a possible recession.
