subtopic: PROVISION FOR DECENNIAL REVISION, EXTENSION OF CHARTERS, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, before the resolution carries I think it is fitting that we examine briefly the whole question of the impact of the banking system on Canada's economy. I should like to give some attention to the suggestion raised by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre and the hon. member for Assiniboia in respect of the necessity in their opinion of having government ownership of the banks to ensure that people will be able to borrow money when they need it.
I should like to ask the hon. member for Assiniboia if he had been running the banking system in Saskatchewan in 1932 and people had come to borrow money from his banks to produce more wheat, would he have loaned freely in order to produce additional wheat and bring down the wheat price still lower than it was in 1932, by increasing the production of wheat? Would he have loaned freely, bearing in mind that a great many of the people who wanted to borrow money would probably never be able to repay it with interest? Would he have loaned money, being quite certain that he would have incurred a loss for his government banks? Not by any means!
Those are two vital points in respect of banking and obtaining loans by ordinary people. May I submit that those are facts which my C.C.F. friends seem to overlook entirely. I do not know that I have ever seen a bank privately owned that would refuse to lend money on a good risk for a good purpose when it looked as though markets and prices were such that the bank in question had a chance to get its money back. I doubt very much that very many banks have been guilty of negligence in that respect. There may be some exceptions.
Fundamentally there is the point for consideration in respect of the question whether or not we should have government ownership of banks. Social Crediters maintain that we do not have to have banks government-owned to ensure desirable borrowing any more than we need to have our coal mines government-owned in order to have coal produced. If there is an effective demand for coal, if there is an effective demand for money, and it is profitable to produce, you

will get money from privately owned banks just as you will get coal from the privately owned coal mines.
While we are discussing this matter let us go just a little further afield and see what it was that was wrong back in 1932. Between some time in 1929 and some time in 1933- I do not recall the dates-$900 million and more were withdrawn from circulation in Canada because the banks called in loans and refused to lend any further. The main reason why they called their loans and refused to lend further was that prices were down so low and markets were so poor that the banks had no certainty of making money.
What should we have done in 1932 had we been adequately managing the banking and financial system along with the economy? Here is a right good chance to ask ourselves that question.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR DECENNIAL REVISION, EXTENSION OF CHARTERS, ETC.
speechtext:
The C.C.F. won't have any
answer.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR DECENNIAL REVISION, EXTENSION OF CHARTERS, ETC.
speechtext: Obviously the answer is to put men to work.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR DECENNIAL REVISION, EXTENSION OF CHARTERS, ETC.
speechtext: How would you do that?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR DECENNIAL REVISION, EXTENSION OF CHARTERS, ETC.
speechtext: By fiscal policy.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR DECENNIAL REVISION, EXTENSION OF CHARTERS, ETC.
speechtext: By what means?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR DECENNIAL REVISION, EXTENSION OF CHARTERS, ETC.
speechtext: By building homes, by building schools, by building roads, by providing employment.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR DECENNIAL REVISION, EXTENSION OF CHARTERS, ETC.
speechtext: That is fine, but all those things cost money.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR DECENNIAL REVISION, EXTENSION OF CHARTERS, ETC.
speechtext: Everything in life costs money, even Social Credit.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR DECENNIAL REVISION, EXTENSION OF CHARTERS, ETC.
speechtext:
If you were administering the government where would you get that money? Where would you have got the money in 1932 if you had been in authority in Canada, as the Right Hon. R. B. Bennett was? Suppose you had had, also, absolute power, as he had not, what would you have done to build those houses and put people to work? There are many fine projects that everybody can think of; even a 10-year-old child can think of what to do if you can get the money.
The Social Crediters maintain that in a condition where you have surplus production -overproduction men called it, all during those years-what you in fact have is a lack of purchasing power, underconsumption. Where you have surplus production the nation can create money debt-free through the government-the minister of finance, against *that surplus production-monetizing it, we call it. A nation can create money debt-free

The Bank Act
as was done under the Finance Act of 1914 and of 1923. Anyone who doubts what I say can go and read the Finance Act of 1914 and of 1923. In the light of the cold facts pertaining to those acts I doubt that anyone will attempt to tell me that what I am suggesting is unsound or contrary to Canadian legal financial procedure all the way from 1868 to 1934. I will challenge any one of the C.C.F. wise men to do that.
We have a lot of men, in the C.C.F. and elsewhere, who can use general terms such as fiscal policy, terms that can mean almost anything under the sun, but when you come to pinpoint their proposals and get right down to see what they are going to do-

subtopic: PROVISION FOR DECENNIAL REVISION, EXTENSION OF CHARTERS, ETC.
speechtext: I gave my hon. friend an example, build schools, build homes, build roads.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR DECENNIAL REVISION, EXTENSION OF CHARTERS, ETC.
speechtext: But what the hon. gentleman did not tell us is where he would get the money with which to do it. Is he going to borrow the money? While this may sound like a little discussion between two groups, fundamentally we are discussing vital points with which we may be faced with utmost painfulness in two or three years right in this parliament. If we do not do a little thinking-through now, before the pressure comes on, we shall not be in the slightest degree prepared to meet the exigencies of a depression when they come. If the C.C.F. movement suggests that the government borrow from the chartered banks the money with which to build the houses, roads, hospitals, schools and all those things which we all agree ought to be built, then that is one approach. But it is impossible to tax the people for money during a depression because they have just not got it.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR DECENNIAL REVISION, EXTENSION OF CHARTERS, ETC.
speechtext: Then print it.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR DECENNIAL REVISION, EXTENSION OF CHARTERS, ETC.
speechtext:
That is going very far down the road to social credit but the social credit line is the right line, and it is the sensible attitude and approach.
If we can agree that printing money may be sound, then that would be some progress. The next question would be, how much can you safely print? How much do you need in circulation at any given time, when do you need it, and when you have printed it, how much do you put into circulation in any given area? And how?
If we are going to have a housing scheme or any of the other schemes, do we require to have our finance minister print the money, or might we better borrow printed money from the Bank of Canada at 2 per cent interest? Can someone tell me why we cannot
borrow it from the Bank of Canada at the 2 per cent interest? I challenge any of the wise men of the Liberal party to tell me why we cannot so borrow it. When the Bank of Canada was established it was capable of taking one dollar of gold and printing four one dollar bills against that one dollar of gold, so that there was only 25 cents of gold backing every dollar bill. But the Bank of Canada at that time was not under the necessity within Canada of redeeming that money in gold because after the suspension of the gold redemption clause in 1933 no ordinary citizen could acquire gold. We should bear these things in mind.
Would someone who knows please tell me why the Bank of Canada could not now take one dollar gold pieces or even one dollar Canadian bonds and produce four one dollar bills on each of them, and loan that money to the government or any other agency in Canada at an interest rate of 2 per cent, especially when that interest would go back into government funds? That is a question which requires to be answered. I would ask my C.C.F. friends to answer that question not in vague general terms but in specific accurate technical terms which will stand up to examination. I am ready to discuss the question with them at any time either in public or in private, and I am also ready to discuss these fundamental principles with the Minister of Finance or any of his wise men.
Let us go back to the question which I raised a moment ago in connection with the sum of $900 million which was withdrawn in the early thirties by the banks calling in their loans and refusing to advance more loans. Why could not that money have been put back into circulation? It is probable that considerations as regards gold had something to do with it, but such considerations should not now have anything to do with the matter as far as I can see. It is a fundamental fact that banks will not lend money to people who are not creditworthy, but except such money is available with which the people can buy the goods and services and the surpluses which at the time exist, then even greater distress is caused, whereas if that purchasing power were available it would serve to bring prices back up and provide work.
I maintain that even if every bank in Canada had been publicly owned in 1932, including the chartered banks, they still would not have dared to lend money until something was righted in the economy. What required to be corrected in the economy? The purchasing power had to be put into the hands of the Canadian people to enable them to buy that surplus production which was then

The Bank Act
available, depressing prices, closing factories, etc. Loans on the part of the banks would have created that purchasing power but no banker would lend the money. That money was there during the twenties and thirties, it was lying in the bankers' tills but it was not being used. Surely no sensible banker would welcome conditions such as that. He wants to lend money and he demonstrated that during the 1940's when we undertook war activities.
I suggest, Mr. Chairman, that if there is one thing the minister should do in regard to this act it is to concentrate his attention on how to manage the banking and financial system so as to make them serve the Canadian people in case we go into a depression. I would also suggest that the one thing which requires to be done in amending both the Bank of Canada Act and the Bank Act is to make provisions whereby adjustments can be made in banking and financial policy in Canada in order to meet the exigencies which will arise in case of a depression.
I have studied every financial measure now before the house and the country; I find no sign of any realization of the need for such a change. For that reason I corn-template our present banking legislation with considerable concern and anxiety. If I might make a specific suggestion I would ask the Minister of Finance in all earnestness -since this is probably the last time he will bring legislation of this kind before parliament-to make provision for the re-enacting of the Finance Act of 1923 as an instrument to be used to supplement the activities of the ordinary banking practices of the chartered banks and the Bank of Canada. If he would do that he would bring into this house and before this country today one of the most hopeful measures that could be contemplated at this time.
When the Bank of Canada Act was passed the Finance Act of 1923 was repealed, and the Finance Act of 1914 was repealed through the Finance Act of 1923. The greatest disservice that has been done to Canada in the past 75 years was done when the Finance Act of 1923 was repealed in 1934. We will never get back to a sound financial basis as far as our mechanics of finance are concerned until we re-enact the Finance Act of 1923 which will give the minister of finance the authority and the power to create money and put it into circulation.
The minister of finance had such power under the Finance Act of 1923 and he had authority to create that money against approved securities of a wide variety.

In the case of the Finance Act of 1914 the minister exercised that power. As I have already this year pointed out, he created $50 million in 1917 and bought Canadian cattle and horses and other commodities and sent them to Britain on loan, greatly to the advantage of Britain and also to the advantage of Canada, and there was no flaw in that procedure.
Sir Thomas White in reviewing the whole matter in his memorandum of dissent, set out at page 85 of the report of the royal commission on banking and currency in Canada published in 1933, tells what remarkable things were done under the Finance Act of 1914 during world war I without inflation. That man went right through eight years during several of which that act was applied. That was the view of a great Conservative minister of finance. It was Hon. W. S. Fielding, the great Liberal finance minister, who caused the act to be re-enacted in 1923, at which time he said he was quite of the opinion that this act would have to become a permanent feature in the financial system of Canada. To my C.C.F. friends I suggest that all they need is the re-enactment of the Finance Act of 1923. Then if the banks will do their part, if the Bank of Canada will do its part and if a wise minister, with a wise government behind him, will use the Finance Act of 1923 re-enacted as a means of supplementing purchasing power, we can weather a fairly severe depression or we can even prevent a depression from coming on.
Resolution reported, read the second time and concurred in.
Mr. Abbott thereupon moved for leave to introduce Bill No. 338, respecting banks and banking.
Motion agreed to and bill read the first time.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO PROVIDE FOR ADOPTED CHILDREN, CHANGES IN ADMINISTRATION, ETC.

speechtext:
The house resumed, from Wednesday, March 3, consideration in committee of the following resolution-Mr. Lapointe-Mr. Applewhaite in the chair:
That it is expedient to bring in a measure to amend the Pension Act to make provision for the payment of additional pension for legally adopted children; to extend the benefits of the act in certain other cases; to provide that the salaries of the chairman, deputy chairman and commissioners shall be fixed by the governor in council; and to provide further for certain changes in connection with the administration of the act.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO PROVIDE FOR ADOPTED CHILDREN, CHANGES IN ADMINISTRATION, ETC.
speechtext:
At six o'clock last night, Mr. Chairman, the minister had finished his

explanation of this resolution standing in his name. I wish to take this opportunity of thanking him for the explanation he gave. I think the material in the resolution will, with some exceptions, meet with the general approval of the members of the house and the veterans across the country. The subject matter will be better understood, of course, when we have the bill before us on second reading, at which time there will be further discussion. We have also been told by the minister that the bill is to be sent to the committee on veterans affairs which is to be set up.
Last night the minister told us that there would be no change in the basic rate of pensions. Whether or not this is necessary is possibly a matter that we need not discuss at the present time. However, there seems to be no great agitation at present for an increase in rate, if we are to judge from the brief which was submitted not long ago by the Canadian Legion to the government. This matter of increase in basic rate was attended to in 1952. At that time some of us thought that the increase was not as great as it should be. As you will recall, Mr. Chairman, there was an increase of 33J per cent over and above the pension which had been set up in 1925.
The resolution is divided into a number of sections. The first section has to do with making provision for the payment of additional pension for legally adopted children. To many of us at different times it had seemed that there was here a rather anomalous situation. The children who were adopted before the pensioner received his pension for his disability were considered to be eligible for pension while those who were adopted subsequent to his receipt of pension were not considered to be eligible. This has been quite hard for a good many people to understand, particularly the pensioner involved.
It was contended, of course-and the minister mentioned this point last night- that there might be something wrong with the adoption, that the adoption procedure in years past was different from what it is at present, that there was danger of babyfarming and so on. I do not think there was too much danger of that as far as the veteran is concerned. As the minister has explained, under our present adoption laws in the various provinces in this country, this danger has certainly been obviated. My opinion is that the veteran at present-and the same would be true of the veteran in the past or the veteran in the future-if he adopts children,
Pension Act
has one or more special reasons for doing so. I am sure the first reason would be that he and his wife like children. Probably they would be in the position where they had no children of their own and realized that a home without children is hardly a home at all. Another reason why the veteran and his wife would adopt children is that they wished to help out some child of their acquaintance who did not have a home, and wished to provide one for it. From experience with people I have known, veterans among others, I have found that often some near relative dies-for instance the father and mother of the children have passed away- and the children are adopted into the home of a brother, sister or some other relative.
As I said before, it was a rather anomalous situation which existed in the past and we are glad that it is being corrected. After all, when we look at the legal aspect of the matter in connection with adopted children, we find that, for instance, they receive the children's allowance and that, under the laws of this country, they have exactly the same legal rights as have other children in matters of inheritance and all other legal matters. The adoption laws in Canada are good despite some unsavoury situations which have arisen in the city of Montreal and other cities recently. We have encouraged adoption of children in this country. A thorough investigation is made to ascertain whether or not a home is fit for adopted children. All provinces have adopted a system whereby a child is not put in a home unless the people who ask for adoption are thoroughly investigated and are vouched for by suitable persons. The home surroundings and conditions are also thoroughly investigated. As I said a moment ago, I am sure there will be no objection at all to this change in our Pension Act.
The minister mentioned the section which deals with the helplessness allowance. I remember that in the committee of 1948, of which I was a member, this subject was fairly thoroughly discussed. At that time the helplessness allowance, which seemed to be and was insufficient, was increased to a minimum of $480 and a maximum of $1,400. At that time there were certain anomalous situations whereby different ranks seemed to be unfairly treated, but that situation was also cleared up to a certain extent. The reasons given by the minister last night I am sure will commend themselves to all of us, namely that many of these men in a helpless condition who are being cared for in their own homes are sent to an institution, and when they leave the institution and go back home

Pension Act
no provision is made for a helplessness allowance. This situation certainly should be corrected, and I am very glad indeed that the minister is doing so.
Another change is to advance the cut-off date as far as marriages are concerned. In the past I have heard this matter argued a good many times in committees. I have heard it argued that there should be no cutoff date, and I have heard very strong and, I think, convincing arguments that there should be a cut-off date. There is a cut-off date, and it is now being changed from 1951 to 1954. The minister mentioned that it was more or less a reflection on the women of this country. I am sure we all agree that the great majority of the women of Canada are what we expect them to be and what they should be. But there has always been a certain class of people known as "gold-diggers", and the purpose of the law is to protect even the old veteran against this type. I think it is well to have a cut-off date, but whether or not 1954 is the proper date will have to be discussed further in the committee.
I remember reading not long ago that in the United States there were widows of veterans of the civil war in that country, which ended in 1866, to whom the government was still paying pensions. The civil war was over almost a hundred years ago. We can benefit by the experience of the United States, and it is just as well to protect our treasury from situations of that kind. But of course very few veterans marry because they want to pass on a pension to someone else. Very often older veterans remarry because their first wives have passed away. They have no one to look after them, and they want to have someone who will take care of them in their old age. I think that type of marriage is a sensible one, and one for which we can very well make provision in the Pension Act.
The third point I wish to discuss has to do with the third provision in the resolution, which provides that the salaries of the chairman, deputy chairman and commissioners shall be fixed by the governor in council. So far as the Pension Act is concerned, this is certainly a drastic change from the existing provision. For the benefit of the committee I should like to read the section of the Pension Act which provides for the payment of the commissioners. It is section 3, subsection 11, and reads as follows:
The chairman shall be paid a salary of twelve thousand dollars per annum, the deputy chairman shall be paid a salary of ten thousand dollars per annum, and each of the other commissioners, including ad hoc commissioners, shall be paid a salary at the rate of nine thousand dollars per

annum: such salaries shall be paid monthly out of any unappropriated moneys forming part of the consolidated revenue fund of Canada.
This provision has been in the Pension Act since its inception in 1928. I am not going to discuss here whether the amounts paid to the chairman and other commissioners are too much or too little. That is not the question at all. This is a change in the principle with respect to payment, and any criticism I have of this provision has to do with the principle and not the amounts. In my opinion this is a matter which should receive the most careful and critical study. There are other acts in which salaries are set out. For instance, there is the War Veterans Allowance Act. I would ask the minister now whether it is the intention to similarly amend the War Veterans Allowance Act.
When an amendment of this kind is being made in the Pension Act I think that to be consistent the minister will have to submit a similar amendment to the War Veterans Allowance Act. If he is going to introduce such an amendment to the War Veterans Alowance Act I should like him to tell us now whether there will be other amendments to that act. Incidentally, so far as veterans legislation is concerned, in my opinion no act requires amendment today more than the War Veterans Allowance Act. The salaries of members of the tariff board, the board of transport commissioners and judges are set out in the pertinent legislation. If a precedent of this kind is to be established, then what is going to be done in these other cases? As far as the commissioners under the Pension Act are concerned, I say that they are more or less in the same category as judges. They hear evidence and judge whether or not the applicant for a pension is entitled to it. In that capacity they act in much the same way as judges, and salaries for judges are definitely set out in the Judges Act.
The action it is proposed to take now removes from parliament the right to set salaries. I think we have already gone too far in this direction. This provision will establish the right to set salaries by order in council. It is my opinion that it is time for a halt to be called to this practice. The more this precedent is followed the easier it will be to follow it. The practice has gone on for so long now that it has become easy for the cabinet or governor in council to assume a responsibility which is really a responsibility of parliament.
Although it is not altogether analogous, I might refer to the indemnities of members of parliament. We discussed Bill No. 171 at considerable length in the house. What sort of situation would we have if the governor

in council had the power to set the indemnities of members? What sort of situation would we have if under the Salaries Act the governor in council had the power to set the salaries of the different ministers? I just point this out to show what I consider is not a healthy situation, and one to which I think we would be justified in calling a halt. I am satisfied, also, that the people of this country do not want any further legislation of this kind. They want the parliament of Canada, the people they sent here, to look after these matters. They are tired and fed up with orders in council and with the governor in council assuming the role of representatives of the people.
There are other changes in the act mentioned by the minister which have reference to administration. I believe I would be fair in saying, Mr. Chairman, that the Pension Act has been and is being well administered. I have said before, and I repeat, that I consider the minister and his department have been very fortunate in having at the head of different branches in the Department of Veterans Affairs men who are good administrators and who, I believe, and know, have been doing a good job.
Whatever changes are made in the administration should and must have careful study. This will be done in the committee, because we have always had very careful study in our committee on veterans affairs. We have before the committee men from the different departments of government, and men from veterans organizations, and all the facts are placed before us. I do not think there should be any change in the administration unless it can be shown to us that those changes are entirely for the benefit of the veterans and their dependents. They are our first consideration. I am sure they are the first consideration of the Department of Veterans Affairs, as they are of all members of the House of Commons. Certainly they are deserving of first consideration by the people of this country.
If I may I should like to revert to the question of salaries. In his opening remarks yesterday the minister said:
Mr. Chairman, in introducing this resolution I should like to state that the proposal to amend the Pension Act at this time does not arise from any changes in the basic rates of pensions paid to disabled veterans, nor does it depart from any of the major principles underlying this legislation.
I claim that this method of raising salaries of officials in the department is a departure from a major principle underlying this legislation. It is a principle that has been in the Pension Act ever since we have had
Pension Act
a Pension Act; and it is there for reasons I have stated before and which I am sure will be stated by some of my colleagues in a better and more concise fashion at a later time.
In the light of these facts, Mr. Chairman, I should like to move an amendment to the resolution as introduced by the minister. I move, therefore, seconded by the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra (Mr. Green):
That the resolution be amended by deleting all the words between the word "cases" in the fourth line, and the word "and" in the fifth line thereof.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO PROVIDE FOR ADOPTED CHILDREN, CHANGES IN ADMINISTRATION, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I do not wish to take up a great deal of time, but I think every veteran in Canada is pleased at the progress being made in eliminating some of the sore points in the Pension Act. I am convinced it is the minister's desire to eliminate all these sore points, and for that reason I should like to take just a moment or two to discuss a point that I think should be ironed out at this time.
In his speech the minister said that-
-under the act as it exists today the wife of a pensioner who is in receipt of a pension of 50 per cent or over-that is, from 50 per cent to 100 per cent-automatically becomes the recipient of a widow's pension of $100.
I think that is fair and proper. However, I should like now to refer to a case that came to my attention recently. We will assume that a veteran is receiving a 55 per cent pension, and that upon his death his widow automatically receives $100 a month. However, if a veteran dies while receiving only a 48 per cent pension, the widow gets nothing at all-nothing whatsoever. To my mind this is unfair. In the case I have in mind the veteran had no other income. He and his wife lived on the 40 per cent pension, just managing to get along. Upon his death, however, the department turned down the widow's application for pension because the act would not permit it, the complete pension having been less than 50 per cent.
I would ask the minister to consider changing this part of the act under which the widow of a veteran receiving less than a 50 per cent pension receives nothing upon his death. I suggest it should be changed so that the widow would receive at least half the pension received jointly by the pensioner and his wife before his death. The widow should not be left with nothing whatsoever. The case I have in mind is too sad to repeat here, although I could give all the details.
I am sure however that similar situations are arising time and again across the country. Before the minister gives final approval to the bill I would ask that he give some support to those widows who are unfortunate enough

Pension Act
to be the widows of veterans who received pensions less than 50 per cent. It may be that those widows are more deserving than the widows of some pensioners who were on 100 per cent pensions. I trust the minister will bear these facts in mind when we proceed further with the bill.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO PROVIDE FOR ADOPTED CHILDREN, CHANGES IN ADMINISTRATION, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I am sure
veterans organizations across Canada will be glad to see this legislation on the order paper, although I am sure some of them will regret that no increases have been mentioned. However, as was pointed out by the hon. member for Royal, there has not been a great deal of pressure put on in the last while in the matter of increases.
The move to place adopted children under the act is in my opinion one of the most important amendments made thus far, because the presence of children in a home is one of the greatest safeguards we could have against neuroses. Undoubtedly their presence would save a great deal of psychiatric treatment that has been found necessary in veterans hospitals. The same observation would apply to people in general, because persons with growing families do not have time to become neurotic.
The hon. member for Royal mentioned the fact that many people like to give homes to children who have no homes. It is a commendable thing, but there is no doubt in the world that no matter how much people can give to adopted children, the children can give them far more. I do think that childless veterans should be encouraged to take children rather than discouraged. Undoubtedly it would help the peace of mind of many childless veterans, and as I said a moment ago the result would be that the government would save a great deal in the long run in hospital care of some of the so-called neurotic cases.
As for the cut-off date, the minister said it was a precaution against deathbed marriages. If it is a precaution I wonder why they keep advancing the cut-off date by three years at the end of every three years. Apparently they have not had too much trouble in that respect or they would not have been advancing the date at the end of the three-year period. If that is so, perhaps the cut-off date is not necessary and other precautions are necessary. We might be able to find some better way of doing it. All the veterans across Canada will welcome the change with regard to the helplessness allowance. I know of several cases where hardship was inflicted on some of the veterans when they were taken off the helplessness allowance.
As for the cabinet taking over the responsibility for altering the salaries of the commission, I do not find too much fault with that. I have always been against order in council government, or the taking of too much power or responsibility by the cabinet. But in this case I do think there might possibly be a reason for a certain amount of flexibility. And although, as I say, I am against the principle of the cabinet taking more and more responsibility and more and more power out of the hands of parliament, I have no particular quarrel with this instance. After all, we are going to have the opportunity to discuss these things on the estimates.
When this bill is sent to the veterans committee, as the minister indicated it would be, I hope the committee will be allowed to dig into the Pension Act, to discuss it thoroughly with the members and with the various veterans' organizations, and that we shall not be held too closely to the amendments brought forward in the bill. We welcome it, but we hope that we shall have an opportunity to dig into the Pension Act as a whole rather than be confined to the amendments in the bill.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO PROVIDE FOR ADOPTED CHILDREN, CHANGES IN ADMINISTRATION, ETC.
speechtext:
I want to say a few words against this amendment and in support of the resolution. It seems to me that some parts of this resolution are extremely important. For years Canada has had the finest veterans' legislation in the entire world, and there are a good many members in this house who have watched the developments over the years and the improvements that we have gradually been able to get who are well aware that that is a fact. That is owing not only to members of one party but to members of all parties. We started out with a not too bad act in the beginning, but we gradually improved it as the years went by owing to the fact that veterans' measures were never considered to be partisan measures in this house, or for that matter in the country.
I for one was very gratified when I heard that there was to be another veterans' committee at this session of parliament. My observation, for what it is worth, is that if it runs true to form of past committees, then the committee will not have any difficulty in finding ways and means of discussing pretty nearly anything that it wants to discuss.
Today I want to mention two particular points. It seems to me that the change in the law to make orphans eligible, on the same basis as other children, for the benefits of the act is one of the finest things ever

done in this House of Commons. I for one entirely approve the sentiments expressed last week by the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam when he suggested that this country, Canada, was big enough and strong enough to be made a haven for all of the homeless orphans that there were anywhere in the world who would be able to grow up in good health and become citizens and assets of Canada. It seems to me that this small piece of legislation that we are now dealing with is symbolic. It may not be a very important thing, and certainly is not a very important thing from the point of view of money, to pass a small amendment to the Pension Act so that orphan children who are legally adopted shall be on the same basis as natural-born children.
As one who in his own modest way has tried for a good long while to have this particular change made, and one who knows a number of families who have gone to the trouble of taking on the care of children not their own, I say that this is a very great thing indeed and deserves the support of the house.
With regard to the rest of the resolution having to do with the fixing of salaries and that kind of thing, I could not care less, because I have every confidence in this government that it will fix the right salaries. If they are to be fixed by the governor in council, it seems to me that that should be all right with this house and all right with the country. We now have the best veterans legislation in the world. I think it is the aim of every hon. member on all sides of the house to keep it that way.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO PROVIDE FOR ADOPTED CHILDREN, CHANGES IN ADMINISTRATION, ETC.
speechtext:
I just
wish to say a word before the resolution passes. I concur in the remarks of the hon. member for Royal and in what was said by the hon. member for Okanagan Boundary. I hope that the minister will say something before the resolution passes about the point raised by that hon. member with regard to the widows of pensioners who receive 50 per cent and over and of the pensioners who receive less than 50 per cent. Perhaps the minister can say why and how it was arrived at that the widow of a pensioner who got more than 50 per cent was entitled to a pension, whereas the widow of a pensioner who received less than 50 per cent was entitled to no pension. The only instance of any explanation that I can recall was that someone in the department made the statement that it was put at 50 per cent so that all application cases would be covered. I think the minister will agree that there are many cases where the widow of a pensioner who is receiving less than 50 per cent pension
Pension Act
needs that pension far more after the pensioner dies than she did during the lifetime of her husband.
I hope that the minister has carefully read -I know he has-the brief submitted by the Canadian Legion, and that his attention has been drawn to the few clauses that deal with the Pension Act, especially section 11 (1) (a), which reads as follows:
Pensions shall be awarded in accordance with the rates set out in schedule A to this act to or in respect of members of the forces when the injury or disease or aggravation thereof resulting in the disability in respect of which the application for pension is made was attributable to or was incurred during such military service.
The minister is well aware that there are many cases that come before the pension commission in which it is found that the disability was pre-enlistment, that it was not aggravated by war service or was wilfully concealed. The comment made by the Legion in their brief is fair and clear and it expresses better than I could the reasons why the government should adopt a different position. They say at page 9:
That section 11 (1) (a) of the Pension Act be amended so that, where a pension applicant who served in an actual theatre of war is found to have disability resulting from an injury or a disease not recorded on his medical examination made on his enlistment, such injury or disease shall be presumed to have occurred or had its inception subsequent to enlistment.
I do not think the minister or any hon. member can quarrel with that suggestion. As the minister is well aware, a soldier is examined by the army's capable and competent medical staff. He is given an X-ray and is marked fit and eligible for service. Surely it is not too much to expect that any injury or disability resulting later on should be attributed to his war service. I should like to direct the attention of the minister to a question of mine which was answered yesterday by the Minister of National Revenue. The question and the answer follow:
Is a pension payable to a widow of a member of the forces under the provisions of the Pension Act capitalized for succession duty purposes?

I think that answer will come as a great surprise to many members of the house, certainly to veteran members. As everyone knows, a pension is not subject to income tax and it seems to me that the widow of any Canadian killed in action should not have her pension capitalized and have to pay succession duties to the provincial and federal governments.
I should like to ask the minister what would happen where a pension is capitalized, the succession duty paid and the widow then

remarries. Under the provisions of the act the pension is cancelled and she receives a lump sum equivalent to the pension for one year. Mr. Chairman, I am not going to debate the subject matter of this resolution because if we were to do that there would not be any necessity for a committee. I have my own opinion as to the changes that are proposed. I emphatically do not agree with the amendment proposed. I am sure the hon. member for Royal will agree that the committee which is to consider the proposed bill should have the right to consider a matter as important as this and debate it in committee. It deserves more consideration than we could give it here. If any amendment of that kind is indicated, it should be after due consideration in committee. I am going to vote against the amendment and I make that statement after consultation with other members of this group who are particularly interested in veterans affairs, including the hon. member for Kootenay West, who is under doctor's orders not to get excited at the present time.
I wanted to let the hon. member for Royal know that, because I think on further consideration he will agree that members of the committee should have an opportunity to debate the desirability of the governor in council setting the salaries of the chairman, the deputy chairman and members of the commission, or whether that should be done by the House of Commons. It is a debatable subject and I think it should be considered by the committee.
Dealing with the resolution itself, there is not very much in the Pension Act that could not be discussed under its terms. As I read it, you could bring in almost anything as they are proposing amendments in the administration of the act. While it sets out specifically one or two instances in which the act is going to be amended, it says also "in certain other cases", which would mean that we would not be restricted very much in our discussions of the Pension Act as such.

I am not going to say very much on the question of the cut-off date for veterans of world war I, as to when a veteran's wife may be considered for pension purposes. I would imagine that there comes a time in a man's life when he needs a nurse more than he does a wife. We can roll this around a bit when we are in committee.
If the matter raised by the hon. member for Okanagan Boundary has not been considered already in connection with other matters, it might be amended in the committee. The widow of a deceased serviceman is protected if his pension was 50 per cent or higher, but if it was 49 per cent, 25 per cent or 10 per cent she has no continuing right. I have always considered that that was an injustice. If a man was 40 per cent disabled his widow had to live with him while he was thus handicapped all his life. Most of them do not save very much money. When such a man passes away the widow receives a lump sum equivalent to a year's pension and that is all. Many of them are in the age group where they cannot work any more and they cannot get old age security or qualify for old age assistance. They are pretty pathetic figures, and while the pension is paid for the handicap suffered by the veteran himself, nevertheless that woman who has spent a greater part of her life living with him also shared that handicap, and whether the figure is 10, 20 or 40 per cent I do not believe it is asking too much to suggest that the government should continue with her share of the pension at the agreed percentage until such time as she passes away. That at least would provide here with some assistance instead of leaving her completely destitute, as any widow would be who has not a continuing right under that act. I would suggest the minister give some consideration to that angle.
There are many things we can discuss in that committee and I rose, Mr. Chairman, to indicate that I cannot support that amendment, because I think any amendments which might be made to this resolution or to the bill can more properly be made in committee after due consideration by members of that committee. My experience with that committee over the years has been that it is pretty sensible, very reasonable, and rather flexible as far as committees are concerned, and it is my hope that the minister will allow us to push him around this time, do important things in this committee, and have features injected into that bill which he does not anticipate at the present time.

Mr. Chairman, this resolution forecasts certain amendments to the Pension Act. I will not go over these proposed

amendments in detail because they have already been discussed by several hon. members.
The first seeks to make provision for children who have been legally adopted, and I believe that would be a very good move, and a move in fact which has been advocated for some years.
The second amendment advances the cut-off date for the marriage of pensioned veterans of world war I. We have extended that date on different occasions; indeed, I believe every time there has been a special committee on veterans affairs. That amendment to the act is also praiseworthy.
Then we have a provision for increasing the helplessness allowances, and that too is a provision which, I believe, will meet with unanimous support.
The fourth amendment dealt with by the minister relates to changes which will facilitate the administration of the act. Apparently there are some changes to be made which will facilitate the handling of administrative problems and streamline the administrative machinery. We really cannot say very much about that until we know what these changes are.
The fifth amendment deals with the question of salaries to commissioners. I shall deal with that in a little more detail in a moment or two, but meantime I would ask the minister to make it quite clear when he replies whether the special committee on veterans affairs is to be permitted to consider any part of the Pension Act.
The government notice of motion calling for the setting up of the committee is to be found at page 11 of routine proceedings and hon. members will notice that the motion refers to certain bills which have already been passed, namely the bill to amend the War Service Grants Act and a bill respecting benefits for members of the Canadian forces, and then it goes on, and these are the words I wish to stress, "such other legislation relating to veterans affairs as may be referred from time to time to the said committee."
I have had the privilege of serving on every special committee on veterans affairs since 1935 and there have been times when the minister, or the chairman of the committee acting for the minister, has taken the stand that the committee could not consider anything beyond the terms of reference. I am afraid that if this notice of motion setting up a committee is passed in the terms in which it now stands, when we try to raise some of these questions which have been raised on the floor today we will be met with the reply, from whoever happens to be chairman, that they are not contained in the bill.
Pension Act
"You can deal only with the sections in regard to adopted children, the extension of the deadline, helplessness allowances and salaries, and anything else is out," we will be told.	!
That has actually happened in the committee on more than one occasion, and I think the minister owes it to the house to make it quite clear today whether he will permit that special committee to deal with anything arising under the Pension Act.
Reverting to the question of the salaries of commissioners and the amendment moved by my very good friend the hon. member for Royal, hon. members will notice that that amendment seeks to strike out of the resolution the words "to provide that the salaries of the chairman, deputy chairman and commissioners shall be fixed by the governor in council."
That amendment brings up two questions and they are questions which cannot be ignored by this house. The first relates to the independence of the Canadian pension commission; the second to the supremacy of parliament as distinguished from the cabinet. I was somewhat surprised to hear my old friend the hon. member for Vancouver South say that he could not care less what was done about this amendment, and he could not care less how these salaries were handled. These two vital principles are principles about which he has been writing in his column for a good many years. I repeat them again: the independence of the Canadian pension commission and the supremacy of parliament.
Why do I stress these two points? Let us look back at this pension legislation. The Canadian pension commission was set up in 1919 under the original Pension Act of Canada. At that time they were called the board of pension commissioners. Provision was made in that original statute for the appointment of a chairman and, I believe, two commissioners. The chairman was to be paid a salary of $7,000 and there was a salary of $5,000 for each of the ordinary commissioners. They were appointed for a set term and they were not subject to change except for cause. Furthermore, the commission was given the widest jurisdiction quite purposely from the start, and that was 35 years ago. It was set up as an independent judicial body in just the same way as our board of transport commissioners was set up, and I suggest in just the same way as the judiciary of Canada was set up. That was the original provision made for a body in Canada to deal with pensions to veterans.

Pension Act
That original charter is of great importance to the veterans of Canada today. They do not want a commission that is subject to pressure by the cabinet. There is no protection at all left for the veterans of Canada if the pension commission is not to be an independent body functioning in a judicial way. The commission was not made part of a department. Under the original legislation it was attached to a department. If hon. members will turn to the Pension Act as it stands today-it is chapter 207 of the Revised Statutes of Canada, 1952-they will find that that provision is still in the act. Section 4 reads as follows:
The commission shall be attached to the department and the expenses required to be incurred for the discharge of its duties shall be paid out of the moneys provided by parliament.
There have been changes in salary. In 1920 the salary of the ordinary commissioners was increased from $5,000 to $6,000. In 1946 the salary of the chairman was raised from $7,000 to $9,000 and provision was made for the deputy chairman to get $7,500 a year and the ordinary commissioners $7,000. Less than three years ago, in 1951, there was another increase. The salary of the chairman was set at $12,000 a year, that of the deputy chairman at $10,000 a year, and that of the ordinary commissioner at $9,000. In each case those changes-certainly since I have been here-were made in the shape of an amendment to the act. There was none of this business of the cabinet making the increase. The changes were made by amendment to the act. The Legion and the national council could come before the special committee on veterans affairs and make representations and there was not any hole-and-corner business about it at all. It was all handled just in the same way we would handle an increase in the salaries of our judges.
The fixed term has now been extended to 10 years. A commissioner holds office during good behaviour for that period and can only be removed for cause by the governor in council. The jurisdiction of the commission is contained in section 5 of the act. I will read the first subsection because it indicates just how wide the jurisdiction is at the present time and how independent this commission is supposed to be. Subsection 1 reads as follows:
Subject to the provisions of this act and of any regulations, the commission has full and unrestricted power and authority and exclusive jurisdiction to deal with and adjudicate upon all matters and questions relating to the award, increase, decrease, suspension or cancellation of any pension under this act and to the recovery

of any overpayment that may have been made; and effect shall be given by the department and the comptroller of the treasury to the decisions of the commission.
What is the meaning of a change such as that which is proposed by the minister? In the first place, I suggest to the members of the cabinet that the commissioners are entitled to have statutory protection in the matter of their salaries. If the minister's change goes through, then the cabinet can reduce the salary of a commissioner if they so wish. They can pay one commissioner $9,000 and another commissioner $10,000. This change puts the commissioners completely under the thumb of the cabinet. That situation is exactly what was being avoided right from the start of this pension legislation. Then on the other hand, if the change is to be used for giving an increase to the commissioners, there again you have the commissioners under the thumb of the cabinet. As a matter of fact the minister explained clearly that increasing the salaries is what he had in mind. In his remarks, as reported at page 2646 of Hansard, he said:
Finally, as the resolution specifies, it is intended to introduce an amendment to permit the salaries of the members of the pension commission to be determined by the governor in council rather than by statute as it exists at the present time. This is really for the purpose of permitting, when it is felt that increases are justified, the commissioners to be adequately compensated without it being necessary to introduce a bill.
That change again puts the commissioners right under the thumb of the cabinet. Why was the board of transport commissioners set up in the other way? Why is it that their salaries are set out in the Railway Act? The reason is, for the one purpose of going as far as possible to make them an independent body. Why do we have our judges' salaries set by statute rather than by the cabinet? Again for the same reason, namely to make the judges of this land independent. If a change such as that which is now sought by the minister is made in the Pension Act, there is no reason whatever why the legislation governing judges' salaries should not be changed so that those salaries also should be set by the cabinet.
I repeat that my first point is that this change strikes at the independence of the Canadian pension commission and that that is a retrograde step of the worst kind. Then, Mr. Chairman, it strikes at the supremacy of parliament. Sometimes I wonder whether the cabinet have any ideas left at all of the importance of parliament, as they are always so ready to belittle parliament or to evade parliament. That is exactly what a change of this kind is doing.

Pension Act
The minister said, "Oh, we will have a chance to have a vote when the estimates are considered". How is that done? A vote is brought in and discussed in the chamber; maybe it is brought forward in the last day or two of the session when there is no adequate opportunity for discussing any vote. It is not considered at all in the other place; these votes are not gone over in that place. On the other hand, if a change has to be made by legislation, there is the opportunity to have it discussed at the resolution stage, as is being done at present; again on second reading; again when the house is in committee of the whole; and again, if necessary, on third reading. There is all the difference in the world between the effectiveness of parliament in passing a vote in the estimates and its effectiveness in passing an amendment to a bill. This change certainly takes away power from parliament. It is another example of order-in-council government. These salaries are to be set by order in council. I am surprised to hear my friend of the C.C.F. arguing in favour of order-in-council government.

Parliament, docile and stagnant-we wonder sometimes why there are so few members in daily attendance. Well, one of the reasons is that, after all, we have become nothing more than a sounding board to legislate and to put through whatever the government decides is for the benefit of the country.
I cannot mention any recent examples; but when members were given their freedom from regimentation to vote on legislation, it was amazingly interesting to watch that vote when one after the other supported the stand taken by the cabinet. I am going to quote from Keeton's book "The Passing of Parliament", and a statement delivered in the British House of Commons on October 23, 1950, upon which occasion the Liberal leader in the British house said this:
It was sad to see how little interest was being taken in a matter that concerned the sovereignty of parliament by members of all parties. During the last thirty years the tendency had been to surrender back to the executive powers that had been won from them over the centuries. There was a tendency to initiate a new judicial power, to create administrative laws, making the executive to a large extent judges in their own case. The sovereignty of parliament was threatened. All the time we were being called on to surrender more and more of our rights and privileges to the government of the day. This continuous erosion was far more dangerous to liberty than any attack from the other side. We were awake to that and could resist it, but the drip, drip, drip of erosion was more likely to destroy the house.
In this country it is no longer a drip. Week after week parliament is asked to surrender its power, to give up its supremacy. What is the minister's explanation for placing the pension board as a pawn in the hands of the government in the manner outlined by the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra? What is his explanation for this change? The minister said:
Finally, as the resolution specifies, it is intended to introduce an amendment to permit the salaries of the members of the pension commission to be determined by the governor in council rather than by statute as it exists at the present time.
Wherein is the statute found ineffectual? Wherein have members of the pension board found themselves paid in lower brackets than otherwise would have been the case but for the statute? And then we have this further explanation by the minister:
This is really for the purpose of permitting, when it is felt that increases are justified, the commissioners to be adequately compensated, without it being necessary to introduce a bill.

Pension Act
Just another surrender to the all-knowing, all-powerful government. Certainly I feel the amendment introduced by the hon. member for Royal had to be introduced at the resolution stage. Where else could it be introduced? Where else could parliament speak-in a committee composed of 25 or 30 members? It is a matter that affects all parliament, every member in the House of Commons. I have mentioned order-in-council government, and the power of the governor in council. I have here an example, one that has nothing to do with pensions, but which indicates this trend to which the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra directed our attention so effectively a while ago. I am going to refer to it because it is a recent example of the sort of thing the governor in council will do if parliament empowers him to do it. When Newfoundland entered confederation, one of the terms in the government white paper entitled "Conference Series 1948 No. 2" was this, dealing with the sales tax on oleomargarine:
The Canadian government will be prepared to submit to parliament legislation designed to exempt oleomargarine sold in Newfoundland from the federal sales tax. in the same manner as basic foodstuffs in other parts of Canada.
That was the undertaking. Today in Newfoundland oleomargarine has no sales tax, because of the fact that the government used the power that it has under order in council. Instead of bringing the matter before parliament they took the back-door method of the order in council, and passed an order in council to the effect that there be a refund of sales tax paid by manufacturers.

When we were interrupted shortly before six o'clock, Mr. Chairman, I was commenting on the real contribution which had been made to the discussion of the national film board by various members of the committee, not only in this group but in others. I should like to refer particularly to the hon. member for Ottawa West and the hon. member for Moose Jaw-Lake Centre. They had sound observations and a worthwhile contribution to make in the way of constructive criticism. It is my intention to refer to some extent also to the speech made on this subject by the Minister of Public Works. In that connection I should like to draw attention to the fact that the minister devoted a great deal of his time to defending the construction of a new building for the national film board and a relatively small part of his time to defending the suggestion that the new building should be in Montreal. I do not know whether it was intentional but it perhaps had the effect of misleading some people into believing that since the major part of his support was given to the suggestion that a new building should be constructed, it was that suggestion that was being criticized by this party and other members of the committee. I think it is well known that practically all members of the House of Commons are of the opinion that a new building should be constructed for the national film board. That recommendation was made by various groups which had studied the problem previously. There is no question as to the necessity for a new building for the national film board. It is definitely a question of where the new building should 83276-170J
Supply-National Film Board be located. I should like to quote briefly from the speech of the Minister of Public Works in reference to this matter. As reported at page 2599 of Hansard he said:
Recommendations that the government should provide suitable and efficient auarters for the national film board have been made for some years now. Hon. members will recall that since 1950 three independent studies have been made of the board's operations. One was by J. D. Woods and Gordon, management consultants: another was by the royal commission on national development in the arts, letters and sciences, and the third was by a special committee of the house which sat in 1952.
After a firsthand examination of the conditions under which the board now functions, all those bodies recommended that better operating facilities should be provided. A specific and unanimous recommendation of the parliamentary committee was that the board's headquarters operations should be centralized in one building specially designed and constructed to meet its production, technical and distribution needs.
In fairness, I must say that the minister pointed out that none of these three bodies made recommendations as to where the new building should be located; but owing to the great amount of time he gave to the recommendations of these various bodies he left the impression-perhaps accidentally; we hope so-that it was to the construction of a new building that objection was taken.
Mr. Chairman, I should like to quote from these recommendations so that there will be no question in anyone's mind as to what was recommended by the various people who made recommendations. I quote first from the summary of principal recommendations of the Woods-Gordon report and action taken thereon, item 11:
The work of the board In Ottawa should be centralized and suitable accommodation provided.
It does not say the work of the board now carried on in Ottawa should be centralized; neither does it say, on the other hand, that the work of the board should be centralized anywhere else than in Ottawa. As I have already quoted, it says:
The work of the board in Ottawa should be centralized and suitable accommodation provided.
When the term "in Ottawa" is used, it is implied, I think, that Woods and Gordon at that time had no intention of recommending that that work should be continued at a later date in any other place. I think it is quite obvious, as I have already said, that there was no recommendation or no hint of recommendation by Woods and Gordon as to where the new building should be.
As to the royal commission on national development in the arts, letters and sciences, they made the following recommendation with regard to the film board premises:
We have observed with anxious concern that the various premises in which the film board conducts its operations are cramped, scattered, inconvenient

Supply-National Film Board and hazardous. In the interests of economy and efficiency, and in justice to film board employees, this deplorable situation should be changed.
We therefore recommend: That safe and efficient premises be provided without delay for the operations of the national film board.
I think every member of the House of Commons, or nearly so, agrees with that opinion that the national film board definitely needs a new and efficient home. But there again the Massey commission report does not hint in any way that it has considered for one moment that that new home should be anywhere else than in Ottawa. If they thought it should be somewhere else, they would have recommended that.
The third group of people who considered this problem was the special committee of the House of Commons which sat almost two years ago. In its report to the house there appears the following:
Your committee inspected the production premises at John street and found that these premises are unsuited to the purposes of the board. Your committee concurs in the recommendations made in survey of organization and business administration report of J. D. Woods and Gordon Limited in March 1950 and by the royal commission on development in the arts, letters and sciences in 1951 that the headquarters' work of the board be centralized in one building designed and constructed especially to meet the production, technical and distribution needs of the board.
There again there is no hint that the committee agreed with the statement that the new building should be constructed anywhere else than in Ottawa.

Mr. Chairman, I wonder if I might rise at this point and ask the hon. member if he was a member of the committee and present on the day on which it was suggested that the board's operations be moved to Montreal.

Yes, I was. I am coming to that matter shortly. What I said, Mr. Chairman, was that in the committee's report there is no hint that they agreed with the information they were given that the board was to be moved to Montreal. Therefore, as far as these three bodies are concerned, it is clear that the question of where the new building should be located was not one of their major considerations, to put the matter mildly. However, the minister was careful to point out-and I have no objection to his having done so-that none of these bodies recommended that the new building should not be in Ottawa. With respect to the arguments advanced by the minister as to why the film board should be moved to a larger centre, I should like to quote what he said in the house on March 2, as found at page 2601 of Hansard. He said:	.
The making of motion pictures is a creative operation. The board must be staffed by people with creative minds behind whom there is a full


head of creative talent. In Canada this creative talent must of necessity come from both our French and English speaking populations. It is abundantly clear from the board's operations over the years that this pool of creative talent is more readily available in the larger centres of Montreal and Toronto than it is in Ottawa. It has been necessary to import much of it here from those centres. Of the two large cities I have mentioned. Montreal is the one with the larger pool of cultural and creative talent in both English and French.
That is an argument that must be considered, but if we are to move the headquarters of one of the activities of government from our capital to any other centre in order to accommodate certain groups of people whose services may be required from time to time it seems to me that it is a case of expecting the mountain to go to Mahomet. That argument does not take into consideration that it will be necessary for a large number of people with talent who are now working for the film board in Ottawa to be moved to Montreal if the new building is constructed there. I do not know whether or not the criticism is just, but it has been observed that that would be the largest forced migration of persons in this part of the world since the expulsion of the Acadians. I think that is putting it rather strongly.
You have been talking to the mayor of Ottawa.
In any case it will mean that a large number of people will have to be moved. Their domestic arrangements will have to be dislocated, and they will have to find new housing accommodation in Montreal.

It is said that Montreal is an area where there is a large amount of both English and French talent and therefore it is suitable that the headquarters of the film board should be moved there because the board's production consists of both English and French films. It can be said that there is a vast amount of talent required in parliament and that our production is in both English and French, and therefore if you follow the argument advanced with respect to the film board to its logical conclusion the day may come when it will be necessary to move the House of Commons from Ottawa. That is again an extreme case, but I think it is following the reasoning to its logical conclusion.
With respect to when the decision was made that the film board should be moved to Montreal, the Minister of Public Works gave a quotation from the brief presented to the special committee by Mr. Irwin, the then

commissioner, which interested me. Mr. Irwin had this to say, as quoted by the minister at page 2601 of Hansard of March 2:
On February 8 last, the minister of resources and development, Hon. Mr. Winters, announced that after detailed study of fifteen possible sites in the Montreal area-
-a certain site was considered suitable. The thing that strikes me about that is that there is no mention made at that early date of examining any other sites. It seems to me that the decision had already been made by somebody prior to May, 1952, that the building would be in Montreal because apparently all fifteen possible sites that were investigated were in Montreal. None of them was in Ottawa or anywhere else. Therefore the decision must have already been made. It is true that some arguments were presented by Mr. Irwin as to the advantages of having the national film board in a large city, but here again it is a matter of degree. He does not say that these advantages pertain only to a city larger than Ottawa or that they all obtain in a city the size of Montreal. During the sittings of the special committee on the national film board of May, 1952, Mr. Irwin was asked the following question, as found at page 88 of the report of the proceedings of the committee:

Your distribution will be made from Montreal?
The Witness: Yes.

What is the reason for locating in Montreal?
The Witness: That is a matter of policy, sir, and I do not know whether or not I should review it.
From a technical point of view is it necessary for you to be in a large city, or is it advantageous?

I think that Mr. Irwin might comment on the relative use to his organization of a large city as compared with some other city. That would be a general type of auestion.
The Witness: As I understand it, sir, these are some of the considerations which lie behind the policy decision. Film production, to begin with, is a manufacturing process, the heart of which is a creative function which has to be manned by creative people. Ottawa, whatever other advantages it has, is a relatively small community and it does not attract many people of the particular kind you need to man the heart of the board's operation. I am thinking of musicians, composers, actors, writers, designers-the whole gamut of the type of people you need in motion picture making.
He went on to say that it was possible that at a future date it would be necessary for the film board to produce films for television broadcasting, and that since the main headquarters of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation were in Montreal it would be advantageous for the film board to be there as well. I do not think it is a valid argument that because one element of our government services is moved to one place you should follow suit with something else. That can
Supply-National Film Board become a vicious thing. It is like the camel getting his head in the tent. It could then be argued at a later time that if we had a national theatre it should not be in the capital because these people with special talents are not in the capital. You could go on from there indefinitely.
The main argument made by Mr. Irwin was that in a larger city you have a large pool of talent from which you can draw. I would be interested in knowing if even now that type of talent is readily available in Montreal. I believe that in the case of recording it is more advantageous to go to New York to have music recorded for films. Therefore the argument is weakened to a certain extent.
I should like to deal very briefly, Mr. Chairman, with some of the arguments which seem pretty apparent to me as to why the film board or, as a matter of fact, most new and expensive buildings should not be located in a very large city. To begin with, the cost of land is extremely high. We have been told already that the land will cost at least $256,000, and it may cost as much as $286,000. The particular site has the disadvantage that it is near an aircraft plant where jet engines are being tested and jet aircraft flown from time to time. The new building will require special sound-proofing to make the operations of the film board possible in that locality.
