Our whole defence against the possibility of a bombing attack from the north is senseless, if that is not a possibility. Therefore it is a very real consideration which must be kept in mind. I think, too, that if we are to have a capital city in our country, the head of every department and branch of government should, if at all possible, operate from that capital.
It is true that the film board is not a department of government; nevertheless it is not very different from a department of government. Governmental departments have top civil servants who are answerable to ministers, and the same is true of the film board. I think every activity of government which has for its purpose the carrying on of some function applicable to the whole country should, if at all possible, have its operations directed from the capital.
I think therefore the arguments advanced back in the nineteenth century when Queen Victoria suggested Bytown as the nation's capital, the capital of this new country, were sound arguments. It was pointed out that Bytown was on the Ottawa river at the junction point of the two great racial groups in this country. And I think the arguments advanced in that day for selecting Ottawa as our capital are equally true today.
As I said earlier, in my opinion every activity of government should be carried on here, if at all possible. After all. if Ottawa is our capital in name it should also be our capital in fact.
The question has arisen as to whether Ottawa would be the No. 1 bombing target in Canada, in the event of an atomic attack. I think this does not enter into the argument, because I would say and recommend that if the film board building were to be built in Ottawa it should not be built right in the city, but rather at some point in the capital area removed some ten or fifteen miles from the Peace Tower. Indeed, I think that principle should be carried out in all of our large cities. We are coming to the place where we would be foolish if we were to place all our eggs in one basket, or to locate buildings where a large percentage of our industrial effort and governmental services could be wiped out by the dropping of just one atomic bomb in the right spot.

So, Mr. Chairman, in closing I should like to quote briefly from the statement made on January 19 by the Prime Minister when he said:
No decision has been reached in that regard-
He was speaking as to the location of the new building.
-but until the government comes to parliament with a definite recommendation for a definite amount to be expended for a building at a definite place there is always a possibility that changes in the recommendation may be made.
I am delighted to realize that. In all sincerity I hope that this statement still stands, and there is still a possibility of reconsidering this matter. In the name of good sense and good government, and in the interests of our national capital, I appeal to the minister to reconsider the matter so that the item may be withdrawn in its present form and a recommendation brought before the house for the building of a new national film board building in the Ottawa area. If this is done I believe it will meet with the sincere approval of the vast majority of members in the house.

Mr. Chairman, as one member from the Montreal district who was very active in urging the government to transfer the main building of the national film board to the Montreal area, I am naturally delighted to think that the government is about to follow through.
I have read with a great deal of interest the debate which took place here on Tuesday of this week and, if I have read correctly, it would seem to me we can all agree as to the purposes of the national film board, that the job it has done up to the present time has been an excellent one, and that the Minister of Public Works is certainly to be congratulated because, having taken over the film board in 1948, when it was at a very low state-and I emphasize the word "low"-he has brought it to a position where most of us will agree that it is a credit not only to itself but to the country as a whole.
Further than that, he was responsible for bringing in Mr. Arthur Irwin, son of the Rev. Alexander Irwin, who became the chairman of the national film board after he gave up the editorship of Maclean's magazine. Under Arthur Irwin certain policies were decided upon and put into force and effect which have brought that organization to the forefront in the production of films in North America. I think that act of constructive policy will be carried out under Dr. Trueman, who is a native son of New Brunswick and a past president of the University of New

Brunswick, and who has given ample evidence of his capacity for the job which he now holds.
If I read the debates properly, I say that the only question that we seem to disagree upon at all is whether the location of the production facilities should be in the Montreal area or should be retained in the Ottawa district. It seems to me that a great deal of agitation on this subject has been whipped up and brought about by a certain few disgruntled employees of the national film board. I should like to refer to a letter which is signed "a film board wife" and which appeared in the Ottawa Citizen on Monday, February 22, 1954. Of course, I am not going to read it all, but one or two extracts will present the point of view of some of the employees-I hasten to add, I am sure not of a majority by any means. It is rather interesting, and among other things the film board wife says:
Any number of reasons have been given proving conclusively that the operation and function of the film board can be carried out far better in Ottawa than anywhere else-in fact, only in Ottawa.
Then she goes on:
There are so many things about Ottawa that we1 love.
And this might amuse the committee for a minute:
To be sentimental, the Gatineau hills across , the river, the sound of the carillon on a hot summer night, Stanley Wong's restaurant, Rockcliffe park on a Sunday morning in January, Byward market in August, Jack Kash's concerts both junior and senior, and the brave new world of the CRT, the flowers that bloom and bloom from April until November everywhere throughout the city, the lions on the post office, the gay abandon of confusion square-many intangible things.
I see she did not put the mayor of Ottawa in there. She goes on:
What lies ahead if we move to Montreal? First, we must sell our house-at a considerable loss . . . then we must try to find another one somewhere on the island of Montreal. Shall it be a jerry-built model in a row of fifty others, all exactly the same? Or shall we live in the slums and have our children play on the streets?
Then later:
Of course, the staff of the film board can huddle together in a tight little inbred bunch-but where then are the great artistic and cultural advantages of cosmopolitan Montreal which seem to bulk so large in the minds of cabinet ministers who insist we should be better off out of civil service Ottawa?
Members of the film board staff are not going to experience any spiritual uplift from working in industrial Ville Saint-Laurent, and since they will be living under worse housing conditions than in Ottawa, this cannot help but affect their work, to say nothing of the strain it will put on family relations.
Who signed the letter?

The wife of a film board employee.

Far be it from me to list here certain of the advantages for those of us who happen to be located in the city of Montreal; but I would say that at least in Montreal we have the advantage of a dual culture and in so far as the town of St. Laurent is concerned we have plenty of good housing, most of it constructed under the National Housing Act. We have plenty of good schools, both regular and separate, English and French and Jewish, and we have one of the oldest preparatory colleges in the Dominion of Canada, namely college St.-Laurent. We have parks and we have churches, and we also have the new member for Dollard constituency, who will certainly be there eager and willing to receive those employees.
I say, further, it is the custom of people who work for private companies and organizations that if the company decides to move its headquarters you go along and move with the company; and if you do not want to move you have the privilege of resigning and looking for a job with greater security and perhaps greater pay elsewhere.
That is it.

We feel that the national film board has expanded far beyond its original purposes. It is true that we are busy making films in Canada, but there is another developing market, namely, the process of making television films not only for the Canadian market but for the growing and vastly superior United States market. I am told that many United States television companies and outlets are now coming in large numbers to the national film board seeking national film board television films because they are better. Certainly, it will be the big business of the future, and part of the job of the national film board will be to produce those good films and also to sell them at a profit.
That brings us right down to the basic question at issue. The film board has grown immensely during the last few years, and the question is primarily one of production and commerce. The problem of location of the production facilities is best solved by locating in Montreal. One of my reasons for that statement is that I believe we shall produce better films because in the city of Montreal, being a large city, naturally we

You have heard, gentlemen, something about our operations and our problems.
What's the purpose behind all this activity?
The Canadian Image
In so great an area as Canada, with a relatively small population, we, as Canadians, can achieve an abiding national identity only if we cherish those things we hold in common while understanding those things wherein we differ-region from region, race from race, interest from interest.
A nation is more than a geographical area. As Canada has proved, it may be more than a single racial group. A nation is a set of values, a belief, a common body of thought.
To fulfil the belief which is Canada, we must steadily nourish the paradox of unity with diversity which characterizes our life as people.
The board's films, I believe, contribute substantially to that nourishment by stimulating in Canadians pride in their achievements, by projecting their growing sense of oneness while portraying their diversities, by interpreting the parts to the whole and the whole to the parts, by holding up images of the Canadian past, the present and the long road that leads to the future.
Canada is on the march to great new achievement. In the film medium, certainly one of the most potent information media available today, only Canadian films can record and interpret those achievements.

The national film board is now truly a national board, not only portraying departmental activities of the government but interpreting Canada to Canadians, interpreting Canada to the United States, in fact interpreting Canada to the world. The national film board has left its purely governmental role and it should seek the larger horizons. With the head office still in Ottawa, but the production facilities located in Montreal, the national film board is taking a forward step to even greater success.

Mr. Chairman, I rise to speak in favour of the amendment moved by the hon. member for Moose Jaw-Lake Centre. I am glad that this amendment does not reduce the vote to $1 because that would eliminate the work being done by the national film board, but it does reduce it by the amount necessary to move the national film board to Montreal. I do not think there is any intention in moving this amendment to say that there is not a need for a central building in which the film board could operate. I think the intent of the amendment is to prevent a move from Ottawa to Montreal. The Minister of Citizenship and Immigration made a statement on March 2, 1954, and I quote from page 2577 of Hansard as follows:
The board therefore presented to us over the past three or four years urgent requests for the construction of a suitable building.
I am sure that there is not one member in this section of the house who would oppose a grant sufficient to carry out that objective. We are vitally interested in how the move to Montreal is going to affect the operations of the national film board. We had some suspicions, and these were confirmed by the hon. member for Mount Royal, who has just admitted that he had considerable influence in bringing about this move. We all know that Mount Royal is near if not in the city of Montreal.
I rose more to refer to the satisfaction which the people of Canada obtain from the activities of the national film board rather than to specifically object or partially object to this move, which I understand is well under way with the awarding of the contract. We appreciate the activities of the film board in making many films available to Canadians living in outlying areas. Otherwise these people would see very few films during the year. The activities of the local film organizations working in co-operation with the national film board have been of great benefit to people in rural areas. I think the national film board is doing a great job and I hope it will do an even greater one in 83276-171
Supply-National Film Board breaking down the isolationist thinking which still goes on in the minds of many Canadians.
The question of bilingualism has been raised. I should be happy to see 300 films made in the western half of Canada with the use of the French language and distributed in Quebec and New Brunswick. With equal satisfaction I should like to see 300 films made this year in Quebec and in the French-speaking portion of New Brunswick with the use of the English language and distributed throughout the rest of Canada. I think through the national film board we can do much more to bring about greater unity in our dominion.
I cannot think of a finer place in which to centre such bilingual activities than the city of Ottawa, where I understand almost half of the people are French-speaking. I cannot see that moving it to Montreal will serve the cause of bilingualism. I agree there are occasions when the people of Quebec are not adequately served by the national film board, but I maintain that they will not obtain better service simply by moving the head offices of the national film board to Montreal. It has been repeatedly pointed out that this move is necessary in order to facilitate production. I observed an admission in this regard by the Minister of Public Works when he said as reported at page 2599 of Hansard of March 2:
While the major part of the board's film work will always be carried out on location in various parts of Canada-
Therefore, when hon. members speak of the production effort I do not think that it matters very much where the headquarters of the film board are located. 1 believe the major production efforts take place in the field in locations anywhere from the Pacific to the Atlantic ocean.
There is one other feature I like about the national film board and that is that it is a relief to see films which do not contain advertising. The films produced by the national film board are such that we can safely send our youngsters to see them and we can recommend them to others. We know that in the production of these films there is no ulterior motive. They are produced in an effort to show Canada to the Canadian people. There is no tinge of propaganda but only the desire to present Canadian situations to the nation.
The film today has to be recognized as a major educational medium and I would like to see, if it is at all possible, the national film board giving a little more support to

I submit that when we are engaged in equipping a great public enterprise that has served the people of Canada as well as the national film board has served us in past years we can afford every cent of this modest expenditure to give the national film board of Canada the finest equipment in the entire world. I for one will be very glad to make Hollywood take a back seat in that particular regard.
What poppycock!

So I find it most remarkable to hear that argument advanced against the expenditure of some $10 million to give the national film board of Canada the plant and equipment to enable it to do a real job. I must say I find that a remarkable argument to come from my hon. friends immediately opposite. One week ago in this chamber we listened to speech after speech from these same members urging and prodding the government to institute a program of public works. They were asking what was the matter with the government, was it asleep on the job or waiting for spring? They wanted a great program of public works. But when we get the first item for something that everybody in Canada from coast to coast knows perfectly well that we need-
Let us have it in Ottawa, not Montreal.	[DOT]

-not on an emergency basis but to do something for the good of Canada,
Supply-National Film Board not for this year, not for next year but for twenty-five or fifty years to come, we have exactly the same group saying that this is gross extravagance and that we should not spend a dollar.
We want it in Ottawa and not Montreal.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: Is this tomorrow's column?

Finally, we have another remarkable argument used: I for one do not believe that the film board was made for Ottawa, nor do I believe that Canada was made for Ottawa. On the contrary, I believe that the capital was made for the country and not the country for the capital. Therefore where we locate any soldier, sailor or airman in our Canadian forces is exactly where that soldier, sailor or airman can best serve Canada. Where we locate the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation or where we locate any agency of the Dominion of Canada is where that agency can do the best job for Canada.
Here in Ottawa.

As a newcomer and freshman M.P. in the house I would not presume to set myself up against the studied advice given time after time by the boards which we selected to advise us exactly how to make this great public enterprise a success. I say that is a very poor way for any party to try to assist a great public enterprise. We have had political parties of different types in this country and in different parts of the country. We have had the Conservatives in Ontario who brought forth that great public-spirited enterpriser, the late Sir Adam Beck, who probably laid the foundation for the political success of the ladies and gentlemen who sit on my left. The Liberal party brought to Canada another great public servant who put the Canadian National Railways on a sound basis and whose only fault was that he was perhaps twenty or twenty-five years ahead of his time. He was criticized by some people for trying to dieselize the road twenty-four years before the United States roads first undertook that modernization.
We have had people who have made public enterprises a success in all parts of the Dominion of Canada, but I must say that it comes as a rather remarkable argument by the hon. member for Moose Jaw-Lake Centre for him to suggest that even though it has been recommended that a public enterprise be moved to a certain part of this great country, Montreal, that recommendation cannot be carried out-

Put it on the record.
2690	HOUSE OF
Supply-National Film Board

-because of the possibility of provincial censorship. The hon. member for Moose Jaw-Lake Centre said, as found at page 2599 of Hansard:
May I remind hon. members that a short time ago Mr. Duplessis, premier of Quebec, suggested that he was going to introduce the censoring of C.B.C television programs. Now, what assurance has the government, if the national film board does move to Montreal, that Premier Duplessis will not decide to censor their work also? I can tell the minister and the cabinet that the people of Saskatchewan will not look kindly upon Premier Duplessis, or any other provincial premier, censoring the kind of film fare they may see; yet if the board does go down to Montreal can the government say this will not take place?
I say to the hon. member that he knew perfectly well when he asked that question that it was sheer downright poppycock and nonsense, that no provincial government in Canada, whether it be the government of Quebec, Ontario, British Columbia, Alberta or Saskatchewan, can step one inch over the jurisdiction of the national parliament and national government.
They did with the C.B.C.

Provincial governments have made fools of themselves in various parts of the country and at various periods of our history. I can remember that when I was perhaps twenty or twenty-five years younger than I am now a Conservative administration in Ontario did not do anything to see that people had the right of free speech even within 100 yards of the legislature in Toronto. I can remember episodes twenty or twenty-five years ago in my hon. friend's province of Saskatchewan that do not look so good when you look back on the history of those times.
Under a Liberal government.
We had in British Columbia not very many months ago an act-

You are going all over the world. Why don't you get down to reality and common sense? You are talking about nothing. You have made no headway at all. We are talking about the film board. Why don't you give your life history?
My point is this^-
What a windbag! You're the best we've ever had.
Thank you for that compliment. My point is this-

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
Order. The discussion on this item has gone far afield. I suggest the


co-operation of hon. members should be given to limit themselves to the subject under discussion.
Thank you, Mr. Chairman. I am coming to my conclusion-
Good.

We have even had in Alberta administrative action by the government forbidding the showing of a product of the national film board entitled "Man-One Family". But I think that should not warp our judgment, that this board should be located wherever the best place is, in the interests of the country.
There is one argument, that whether we like it or not this country is a two-language, two-religion and two-race culture; and I think that we can live together, that we can prosper best and that we can go forward best if we accept the spirit of that situation. And one reason I think for the great success of the party on this side of the house is that, over the generations, it has accepted the spirit of that underlying basis of confederation perhaps better than some other political organizations have. And, whatever else we do or do not do, let us hope to have the national film board where it will do the best job for all the people of Canada-and by "all the people of Canada" I mean all the people of both cultures.
Mr. Chairman-

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
The hon. member for
Yorkton.
Go ahead.

Mr. Chairman, I was observing closely while the hon. member for Vancouver South was making his remarks, and I noticed that the Minister of Finance interrupted the reading of his newspaper long enough to converse briefly with the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration. I wonder if the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration is now in a position to answer the question which he said earlier was really one having financial implications rather than one for his department.

speakerposition: Minister of Citizenship and Immigration; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: I am sure the hon. member for Kamloops is not in a position to do mindreading, on this side of the house at least. It was I that conferred with the Minister of Finance, and not he with me; and our conversation was one which I am sure the hon. member would not like to hear.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: Very smart!

There are lots of conversations over there that we do hear sometimes, but that are not very enlightening. So what

passed between the two ministers, in the light of the minister's remark, perhaps could be left for the public to judge.
However, the Minister of Finance is here, and-

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: -has finished his paper.
Could he tell us what the implications are of this move to Montreal, so far as employees of the film board are concerned, with respect to income tax?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I have not the faintest idea, Mr. Chairman.
And you care less.

Well, that is obvious. My hon. friend from Simcoe North merely draws attention to the obvious. Does the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration, then, not consider that perhaps the move to Montreal should be delayed a while, and this item therefore eliminated while the implications are being considered and the matter possibly straightened out?
He cares less, too. So, why talk about it?

I have listened with great interest to the hon. member for Vancouver South. Listening to the hon. member one would almost think that the C.C.F. group had suggested that we should not spend money on a building for the national film board. That was the basis of the hon. member's argument. I would point out to him that we have supported a building for the national film board, but we want it built here-and I think he knows that very well.
You know, Mr. Chairman, his speech reminded me of a little poem that goes like this:
You cannot hope to bribe or twist,
Thank God, the British journalist.
But seeing what the man will do unbribed, There's no occasion to.
And I think that probably fits him quite well. The protests which have followed the news that the government is moving the national film board from Ottawa to Montreal show that you can push the Canadian people too far. These protests do not come only from Ottawa. You cannot always measure public reaction or opinion with an engineer's slide rule.
To give an illustration, my constituency is located almost two thousand miles from here. I have received resolutions from very responsible groups in my constituency of Yorkton who are interested in the value of the educational work the film board is doing. To some people this interest might seem
Supply-National Film Board strange, but it is an indication of something that is very important. I am pleased to know that they have protested, and I was pleased to receive a request from them to rise in my place in the House of Commons and express their protests against this move by the government. My people are protesting against the removal of this fine organization, the film board, with its record of progress, and its establishment here in Ottawa for a number of years. It is an organization just reaching its full vigour of maturity and manhood which, suddenly, finds that it is torn up by its roots and moved to Montreal.
My people are asking the reason for all this. Why is it being done? What is behind this? Has there been a clear statement of government policy? Who started it? Have they studied the full implications of their actions? I am pleased, as I say, that the Canadian people are alert to an injustice. Naturally they imply-because they have been given no information to the contrary-that some concessions must be given to some people, or some personal privileges handed out here or there. They know that that part of Canada sends a pretty solid bloc to support the government in Ottawa at every election- irrespective of what they might do provincially, when they send a solid bloc to support the Duplessis government in Quebec.
The manner in which the government has carried out this piece of administration is, in my opinion, pretty bad, and they will reap the results.
And that is what the hon. member for Ottawa West said.

The maintenance of unity is a matter of great concern to every government in Canada; that is one of the things that make the maintenance of government an unpredictable thing in this country. It is an odd experience. And this government is responsible for stirring up all kinds of suspicions that something is wrong. The people would prefer to have a forthright statement right from the beginning. They would ask the government what it intends to do and what arrangements have been made-instead of allowing all these rumours to be circulated across the country from coast to coast. The protests being made from all parts of Canada are a clear sign that something is wrong. We have tried to get forthright answers from the government ever since the session opened last November, at which time members in the opposition asked the government what was going to be done. The reply was, "Oh well, the matter has not been finalized", and "the contracts have not been let."

Supply-National Film Board
The whole matter of the effect which this will have upon the established people who have helped to build the film board is an important matter. It cannot help but have an effect upon them, since it will mean tearing up by the roots what they have established over the years. It will have an effect on the education of their children, since they will be leaving places where they have established themselves and where they have felt secure, where they have been able to build the kind of home they like. The morale of these people is very easily destroyed by moves such as this.
Tonight an hon. member from Montreal said that if we decide to move they can come along or they can quit. Such an attitude is scarcely the one to adopt toward senior civil servants who have abilities and qualities which are of a high order and of the calibre required to do the kind of delicate job that is undertaken by the national film board. I can only say that the whole thing has been ill-conceived, poorly timed and miserably executed.
It is very harmful to the good work that the national film board has done and it disturbs, to a greater degree than the government probably realizes, the balance that is required in Canadian unity. It might have been avoided if this government had come out with a policy in the early stages and had given a forthright statement of policy right from the beginning to the end.
I want to tell this government that there are some things, such as the feelings of people, and ideas that lie in the minds of people, which are dear to them, and when they are hurt, it takes a long time for the wound to heal.

When the hon. member for Vancouver South spoke he said to hon. members that what we should do is to let the members of the national film board pick out the site, do this, that and the other thing. He said that they had studied the matter and they knew all about this project. The hon. member did not tell us what a mess the members of the national film board made of the national film board before 1948 when the Gordon report was brought in. If the members of the national film board were the same as those previous to 1948, I think he would agree with me that the decision as to the change should be left to parliament.
I was glad that the hon. member for Mount Royal mentioned that, before the present minister took over, the national film board was at a very low ebb. I said that he had better not let the Minister of National Revenue hear him say that.
[Mr. Castleden.I

The minister said that the site for the film board in Montreal was going to cost $240,000. I think that is the figure he gave us the other day. The city of Ottawa offered a site free.
I have one objection to the moving of the film board to Montreal. I am afraid that by moving the national film board to Montreal its activities will not be watched as closely as they should be by the minister. He will not have the opportunity or the time to be running back and forth.
This afternoon I mentioned the director who was put in to clean up the mess. I will say this-I said it a year ago-that he did a good job; but I do object to the way in which he was engaged, with a plum hanging out on the end of the limb to the effect that if he did a good job, at the end of three years-
That is no more accurate this evening than it was this afternoon.

If it was not
right, then how is it that three years before it happened I asked the minister if it was going to happen and he said no. And three years afterwards, almost to the day, the gentleman was appointed to a diplomatic post. I say, more power to him. But if he retires after five years he has a pension for life. That was quite a nice plum to hang out, and I hope that the present director of the national film board worked out a bargain with the minister that is just as good. If he did, he is a good man.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order. May I also say that these remarks are about as much in order this evening as they were this afternoon.

I agree with you, Mr. Chairman. Since you have said that, I will not say any more about it.
In the public accounts for 1953 there is an item of $306,892 for removal and travelling expenses. I just wonder what that item will be after this film board building is put up in Montreal. It will be triple that or more. It cannot help but be that much.
When he spoke the minister said that in the United States the different departments of the government were spending more than the film board spent here. The minister did not say that the different departments of the government of the United States pay their own way. They do not get buildings absolutely free. I understand that the buildings they occupy in the United States are charged up to them, but they are not charged up to the national film board here. The national film board in this country does not pay rent for the buildings or anything of

that kind. All they pay is their operating expenses and what they purchase. I should like to ask the minister a few questions. He mentioned the New York architect who had been engaged. Will the minister tell us what has been paid to that architect so far, and what arrangements have been made with him? The minister mentioned on April 9 that they did not have the plans of the building. But in Mr. Irwin's report of 1952 I find this:
The minister added that plans for the proposed building were being prepared by the Department of Public Works. It is expected that these will be available during the current fiscal year.
That was the fiscal year 1952-53. I want to know whether the minister was right or wrong when he said on April 9 that he did not have the plans.
Of which year?
Of last year. The minister said in 1952 that he did not have the plans, but that they were being prepared.
One minor point: the Minister of Public Works said that on April 9, 1952; but there is another Minister of Public Works today. However, he was correct in the statement he made at that time.

Well, if he was correct at that time, why did the minister not have the plans last year? I think the minister is wrong, because in the paragraph preceding the one I just read, these words appear: "Hon. Mr. Winters". I think that is the Mr. Winters sitting opposite me now.
I should like to know what it costs to rent the nine buildings here in Ottawa, as well as the two storage buildings which the minister mentioned the other night. What does the char service cost-as Minister of Public Works the minister should know this -for these buildings? I do not believe the government carries any insurance on the buildings, and if there is a fire, everything will be gone. Some of these buildings are rented and I believe some are owned. I should like to know what the upkeep charges on these buildings are. I should like to know if the department has figured out what will be the cost of the upkeep of this new luxurious building in Montreal.
It is not luxurious.
It is a luxurious building in every sense of the word; it cannot be anything else at that price.
It is minimum accommodation.

What about the pool?
Supply-National Film Board

I should like to know what the upkeep cost will be. What will be the carrying charges? There will be interest on the money expended and I should like to know just what that will be. I have asked about the char service. What will be the total cost of the upkeep on the new building, and what is the total cost of the present buildings?
I have said this before, but I repeat that I sat in on the national film board meeting and I sat in on the public accounts committee. I feel that the national film board should be placed on a sound business basis in every way so the people of Canada will know exactly what is being spent. The public works department absorbs the cost of char service, rentals and everything else, and I feel that those should be charged to the national film board as well as interest charges on the money expended. I feel that it is due to the people of Canada that that should be done.
I said last year, and I shall not repeat it, that the film board is doing a good job. I said also that I thought it was on a better basis by far than it had been before. It provides something that the people of Canada need, something that they want, but they want to have this board run properly. When this matter was brought up on Tuesday there seemed to be some misunderstanding as to the distribution functions of the film board. I believe tonight one hon. member mentioned the fact that it was a great boon to the rural people.
From what I can see, from what I have heard, and from what I have read, I believe that the people in the urban centres of Canada benefit just as much as those in the rural sections. There seems to be some understanding also both in and outside the house with regard to the distribution of films and the work of the film councils that are set up. The national film board has a man in each district who is paid a salary plus living expenses. I believe these men are doing a pretty fair job. They set up the film councils. These councils have nothing to do with the board, except that the district man guides them along their way.
I know that in my own city of Peterborough those who wish to belong to the council pay $2.50 per year. They are allowed to have what films are in the library, and if they are brought from outside they pay the shipping charges or whatever it may be. It may cost them fifty cents a night for a film, or it may cost $4 or $5.
There is also a film council in the county. There is one school in which I am interested

Supply-National Film Board that pays $20 to belong. The district man comes up about once a week to show films and it is worth it. They are doing a good job. It is not only national film board films that are shown; films produced by different companies in different countries are also shown. In most cases they are educational.
I am afraid that the chairman may call me to order on this, so I had better not say anything more. I repeat, I am afraid that if this move is made to Montreal the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration, who is now responsible for the board, will not be able to keep his finger on it as he should. We do not want this film board to get out of hand, as it did, and grow up like Topsy.

This is an item to cover part of the cost of a new building in Montreal and I have not before me the figures on the char and other maintenance service for the buildings here in Ottawa occupied by the film board. I am speaking from memory and subject to correction, but I believe the fee to John and Drew Eberson was $35,000. I wonder if the hon. member would be satisfied if I got the other information and gave it to him when the first item of public works is before the committee.
That will be quite satisfactory.

Mr. Chairman, it has become quite a habit in this house-sometimes I have fallen into it myself-that when an hon. member rises he says that he has been listening with a great deal of interest to the speeches that have been made. But I must confess tonight that I cannot pull that one this time because I have not listened with very much interest to any of the speeches that have been made on this matter of transferring the film board from Ottawa to Montreal. I was interested in the minister's reply, and I considered it a rather weak attempt to give a reason for the move. But I really have not been able to work up too much interest in the subject.
One or two hon. members have said that they have received many protests from all over the country. I am not going to doubt their word, but frankly I do not believe the people outside of Ottawa and Montreal care one snap of their fingers where this film board is located. I do not think the people in Macleod constituency care where it is located. As for receiving protests, I have not received one. I have inquired of some of my colleagues around here and they have not received any either. Of course we come from the two western provinces and the matter may be so geographically remote that we do not expect them to do much protesting.


There are one or two things I should like to say since this is an item respecting the national film board. In years gone by I have been somewhat critical of the national film board and also of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation, while at the same time I have tried to be fair and admit that in a measure both these organizations are trying to do a good job. As far as the films turned out by the national film board are concerned, I believe they have done some pretty fine work. However, when it comes to films of a dramatic nature I do not care how much we spend on a building or how much hon. members talk about the various cultures that are to be found in Canada, and whether there is more culture in Montreal than in any other centre. I do not believe there is. I believe there is just as much culture in any other great metropolis in Canada as there is in Montreal. I follow some of the cultural programs on the radio and I must admit that Montreal has its fair share of dramatic talent, but there are other places in Canada, and I am thinking of Winnipeg, where there is equally good dramatic ability. As regards the dramatic arts, Winnipeg must rate very high indeed.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: Hear, hear.
I do not include the political arts.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: It is higher still when it comes to that.

As regards the city of Vancouver, I will say that it must rank pretty high when it comes to the dramatic arts. You can listen in to the radio as well as visit the "Theatre Under the Stars" during the summer and you will hear and see some pretty good productions. An hon. member here suggests Toronto, and I can say "Amen" to that. As regards the dramatic arts, I wish the film board well in their efforts, but if they are ever going to attempt to compete with Hollywood productions or some of the J. Arthur Rank productions then they have another think coming. Never in the wide world will they be able to surpass the productions of the major motion picture industries of the United States and Great Britain. However, when it comes to publicizing Canada, I believe that is where their main effort may be most effective. The series "Canada Carries On" has been of tremendous value to Canada. The series "Eye Witness" are excellent productions. But I have some limited criticism to make of the "Eye Witness" productions. I do not like the first scene of "Eye Witness" when the picture opens and you have to look twice to see what that thing

is. After you look a few times you gain the impression that it must be the lens of a camera-and it is.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: The hon. gentleman may remember that a short time ago I considered it my duty to point out to a previous speaker that we are discussing the construction of a building for the film board and not the production of films. I would be glad if the hon. member would confine his remarks to the matter under discussion.

Thank you, Mr. Chairman, for drawing that to my attention. I should have been wise enough to recognize that. However, you have stopped me at an extremely interesting point and I would like to know whether, if the film board is moved to Montreal, we will still have to look at that lens, and whether we will still have to look at what appears to be a relief map. When I first saw that map I thought I was looking at someone's cancerous liver, and on a second glance I found I was looking at a relief map of Canada. If that is changed, the "Eye Witness" productions will be much better.
I have only a few minutes left, Mr. Chairman. I would like to emphasize that the film board has not only the responsibility of producing good pictures, but also the responsibility of depicting, if possible, the glories of our free and democratic way of life. That, Mr. Chairman, is a tremendous responsibility. In days gone by there has been some feeling on the part of several hon. members that perhaps the film board has not been doing its job along that line. In addition, the minister has not given a reason that will satisfy me for moving the board to Montreal. I will project my own reason, and I do not know whether I am far out. I believe they want to get the board away from this parliament. I believe they regard members of parliament as being capable of learning too much if that institution is located near where we operate.
Oh.
Some hon. members say "Oh," but that does not impress me in the least.

That is all some of them can say.

An organization such as the national film board is one of the most powerful media of thought and propaganda in the world, and I believe the government thinks that members of parliament should not be too close to the scene of operations lest they learn too much. I base my opinion on what I believe is a very important principle. The hon. member for Kamloops asked a few questions the other day and was unable to obtain answers.
I did not get the answers tonight either.

Subversives have operated in various democratic countries and my bet is, Mr. Chairman, that they have not overlooked the most powerful medium of propaganda which is operating in this country and in the world. They are not so foolish as to overlook that. One might ask "What are you inferring?" But what can I do but infer? I cannot get any information.
Ten o'clock.
My hon. friend from Lambton West calls it ten o'clock, Mr. Chairman, and for him I would ask you to call it ten o'clock.
